articles.title: Inspiring story of the day: “She could have stopped me a long, long time ago, but she didn’t” - How Roger Federer turned a 22-year partnership with his wife Mirka into tennis perfection
articles.summary: International Sports News: Roger Federer’s career ended with 20 Grand Slam titles, eight Wimbledon trophies and 103 tour-level titles, but his final farewell was not really abou.
articles.body: Roger Federer’s career ended with 20 Grand Slam titles, eight Wimbledon trophies and 103 tour-level titles, but his final farewell was not really about the numbers. At the 2022 Laver Cup in London, Federer broke down while thanking his wife, Mirka Federer, for standing beside him through the hardest parts of his career. Their relationship began at the 2000 Sydney Olympics, when both were young tennis players. More than two decades later, Mirka was still beside him as he played his final match. Federer’s own words showed just how much that support meant to him.How did Roger Federer and Mirka Federer first meetRoger Federer and Miroslava “Mirka” Vavrinec met at the 2000 Sydney Olympics, where both represented Switzerland as tennis players. Federer was only 18 at the time, while Mirka was already competing on the professional circuit.Their meeting happened before Federer became the global tennis star that fans would later know. At that point, his career was still taking shape. Mirka, meanwhile, had her own ambitions in tennis and had competed at Grand Slam tournaments.Their lives changed when Mirka’s playing career was cut short by a foot injury in 2002. She had reached a career-high ranking of No. 76 in the WTA singles rankings, but the injury meant she could no longer continue competing at the same level.From there, Mirka remained closely connected to Federer’s tennis life. She became a familiar presence in his player box and travelled with him during a career that took the family around the world.Federer later married Mirka in 2009. Their partnership grew alongside his rise to the top of men’s tennis, giving their relationship a rare link to almost every stage of his professional career.What role did Mirka Federer play during Roger Federer’s careerIt would be too simple to describe Mirka Federer only as Roger Federer’s wife. She had been a professional tennis player herself, so she understood the demands of the sport from personal experience.As Federer’s career became more demanding, she stayed close to his daily life on tour. She was often seen watching from the stands and became part of the small family unit that travelled with him.Federer’s career eventually stretched across 24 years. He played more than 1,500 matches, spent 310 weeks at No. 1 and won 20 Grand Slam singles titles. The ATP Tour also records 103 tour-level trophies, numbers that show how long and demanding his career was.That long run also came with injuries, defeats and difficult decisions. Federer announced in September 2022 that the Laver Cup in London would be his final ATP event after repeated knee problems prevented him from returning to full competitive fitness.The most important point about Mirka’s role, however, came from Federer himself. He did not describe her support as something distant or ceremonial. Instead, he connected her directly to his ability to keep playing.How did Roger Federer describe Mirka Federer at his final matchFederer’s final professional match came on September 23, 2022, at the Laver Cup. He played doubles with Rafael Nadal against Jack Sock and Frances Tiafoe at London’s O2 Arena.The match ended in defeat, but the result quickly became secondary. Federer had already said the event would be his final ATP appearance, and after the match he became emotional while speaking about his family.Looking toward Mirka and their children, Federer said:“My wife has been so supportive… She could have stopped me a long, long time ago, but she didn’t. She kept me going and allowed me to play. It’s amazing. Thank you.”The words mattered because they came at the end of a career that had demanded years of travel, training and recovery. Federer was not simply thanking Mirka for being present at one final match. He was recognising the support that had continued through the many years before it.He also thanked his parents, Robert and Lynette, during the farewell. His family had been courtside for the emotional ending, making the moment much more personal than a normal retirement ceremony.Federer later spoke about the evening as a “perfect journey” and said he would do it all over again. The ATP Tour reported that Mirka, their children and Federer’s parents were all watching from courtside as his professional career came to an end.Why does Roger Federer and Mirka Federer’s story still stand outFederer and Mirka’s story stands out because their partnership grew while his tennis life was becoming increasingly demanding. They met when Federer was still a young player. They married before he completed much of his record-breaking career, and Mirka remained part of his life through his biggest wins and his eventual retirement.The couple also raised four children: twin daughters Myla and Charlene, followed by twin sons Leo and Lenny. Their family life developed alongside Federer’s international career, which required constant travel and long periods away from home.There are several quotes often shared online about Federer’s family life, including claims that he “could not sleep without my wife” and that Mirka “made that nomadic life feel like a real home for our children everywhere we went.” Another widely circulated quote has Federer saying:“When I met her, I had zero titles. Today I have over 100. She’s been with me through every single victory and every defeat. She built my schedule, packed our bags, and took care of everything so I could just focus on playing the game I loved.”Those longer quotes could not be independently verified in reliable primary or major sports sources during this fact-check. For that reason, they should not be presented as confirmed Federer remarks. His farewell comments about Mirka, however, were directly recorded after his final match and are well documented.That distinction matters. Federer’s real words were already powerful enough. He had spent years collecting trophies and records, yet when the moment came to speak about the people who helped him through the journey, his attention went to his wife, children and parents.His final tribute to Mirka also explains why their relationship remains an important part of Federer’s story. His career was built on extraordinary tennis, but it was not lived by him alone.Federer finished with 20 Grand Slam singles titles, including eight at Wimbledon, and retired as one of the defining players of his generation. Yet his farewell showed another side of that career: the person waiting beyond the court, supporting him while the cameras focused on the champion.For Federer, Mirka was not simply watching the journey. She was part of it. And when he finally said goodbye to professional tennis, he made sure the world knew it.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Mensik and Muchova Beat Bencic and Cobolli to Win $1M US Open Mixed Doubles Bracket
articles.summary: Ahead of the U.S. Open singles tournament starting on Sunday, Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik got an early start on what they hope will be successful runs by winning the mixed doubles tournament.
articles.body:
Ahead of the U.S. Open singles tournament starting on Sunday, Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik got an early start on what they hope will be successful runs by winning the mixed doubles tournament.

Muchova and Mensik, who overcame two match points in the semifinal earlier in the day, defeated Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli 6-3, 1-6, 10-6 at Arthur Ashe Stadium on Wednesday night to win the trophy and $1 million prize.

Muchova and Mensik trailed 9-7 in the tiebreak in their semifinal matchup against Andrey Rublev and Mirra Andreeva before winning four straight points to reach the final.

They were able to carry that momentum into the start of their showdown with Bencic and Cobolli by winning the first set in nine games. Bencic and Cobolli rebounded with an impressive 6-1 victory in the second set to force the tiebreak.

The tiebreak went back and forth between the two pairs before Muchova and Mensik eventually pulled away, culminating with Mensik's ace on championship point.

Wednesday's win marked the first Grand Slam title in any competition for both Mensik and Muchova.

Mensik, who will turn 21 on Sept. 1, has never reached the final at any of the four major tournaments as a singles competitor. His best showing at the U.S. Open has been two appearances in the third round.

"It's my first time standing here," Mensik said after Wednesday's victory. "I didn't expect this before the tournament, but it's such great fun. It was amazing to play and start the US Open like that."

Muchova has two Grand Slam finals appearances in her singles career with the most recent coming at Wimbledon earlier this year. She lost to Linda Nosková in three sets.

Mensik will enter the men's singles tournament as the No. 18 seed. Muchova the No. 7 seed in the women's tournament.

The singles draw will be held on Thursday, leading to the start of the tournament on Sunday.

articles.title: Wyndham Clark is having a career year after a terrible 2025. Now all he wants is to be loved
articles.summary: The reigning US Open champion, who is sitting in third place in the FedEx Cup standings heading into this week, is enjoying his best year as a professional.
articles.body: Wyndham Clark just wants to be loved. The reigning US Open champion, who is sitting in third place in the FedEx Cup standings heading into this week, is enjoying his best year as a professional. Last week’s victory at the BMW Championship outside St. Louis was his third win of the year. But he’s noticed a trend with those three victories, as well as the three others that preceded them earlier in his career. “You know, what’s funny is I’ve now had six wins, and I think in all six of those wins I was never the crowd favorite,” he said to reporters at Atlanta’s East Lake Golf Club ahead of the season-ending Tour Championship that tees off on Thursday. “I always heard other people’s cheers. Maybe one day I’ll be who everyone is rooting for.” And it’s not just on the course that he’s hoping to feel the love. One reporter in Atlanta was taken aback when Clark said part of his off-season plans is to “hopefully get engaged.” “What do you mean, ‘hopefully’?” the reporter asked. Clark replied, “Hopefully she says yes.” It’s the sort of humility that comes with seeing your career bottom out a little more than 12 months earlier, sometimes in embarrassing fashion. One year before his triumph in the 2026 US Open, Clark missed the cut at the same tournament and took his frustrations out on the Oakmont Country Club locker room, causing enough damage that the famous club outside Pittsburgh banned him for life. It was the low point of a bad year for Clark. He’s not exactly a fan favorite on tour, owing in part to those actions at Oakmont – his victory at Shinnecock Hills in New York was lamented by some golf fans who didn’t want to see him march to another major championship. He was also the subject of some Zapruder-esque investigation on social media after a pre-shot routine during his final round on Sunday at the BMW. Clark took out multiple clubs and tested how they felt in the grass behind his ball after an errant drive on the 14th hole, something he called a routine move for tour players. Internet sleuths accused him of trying to improve his lie in the rough, similar to allegations against Bryson DeChambeau at the British Open last month. Clark denied the accusation, saying, “I never fully put the club down behind it. I don’t think anything of it.” “When the cameras are on you, they’re going to find anything. And I think you saw that in Bryson’s case. It happened to me at the U.S. Open, it happened to me at Bay Hill,” he added. “It’s happened to a lot of guys where they can see stuff that maybe looks like something that maybe it’s not. That lie was never bad. It was more just judging what it was. By no means did I take a bad lie and make it really good. People can think what they want. I know I didn’t do anything that was costing the integrity of the field. That’s all I’ve got to say about that.” Even so, as the 2026 season comes to an end, Clark is not taking the route some other athletes in his situation might choose – embracing becoming the villain. Instead, Clark appears eager to embark on his own version of a redemption tour, one great round of golf at a time. In a sport like golf, where grinders like Clark are revered, that sort of head-down, do-the-work attitude may be what ends up appealing to fans. “I’d say the No. 1 thing is resilience,” Clark told CNN Sports’ Patrick Snell when asked what clicked for him this year. “Obviously, ’25 was a tough year. I had to deal with a lot and I felt like I got through it the best that I could. And then I bounced back. “I think one of the greatest things you can do in life and in sport is to – when you get knocked down, how do you handle it? And it wasn’t easy, but I handled it the best I could, and I’ve been very blessed that I have a great team that helped me get back to where the point I am now, and now I feel like I’m set up to continue to have success the rest of this year, but also in the future years.” That work is mostly being done quietly now. The few fans following Clark around in the baking heat of the Atlanta afternoon on Wednesday paled in comparison to the flock strolling alongside world No. 1 Scottie Scheffler a few holes ahead. As he practiced with fellow pros Robert MacIntyre and Matt Fitzpatrick, Clark worked his way around the course, testing putts to different hole locations and hitting shot after shot out of East Lake’s white sand bunkers. He signed a few autographs, hit a bunch of putts and went through an otherwise workmanlike practice round. In his interview with CNN Sports, he pointed to a new swing coach and a new putter as key factors in his resurgence this year. “It’s always the chicken or the egg. Is it mental (issues) that led to bad physical, or physical to bad?” he told Snell. “And I kind of chalk it up as more physical. And after making those two changes, I started seeing good golf, which then led to more confidence, which then led to winning, which led to more great golf and now we’re here.” It was a sign of what Clark believes will sustain his success – and perhaps convert a few skeptics along the way. “It’s a validation of knowing that all the hard work I put in is paying off,” he said.

articles.title: Alcaraz se estrena con Safiullin en el US Open y podría medirse a Djokovic en las semifinales
articles.standfirst: Rafa Jódar, que circula por la parte alta del cuadro, se las verá de inicio con el australiano Kokkinakis
articles.summary: Rafa Jódar, que circula por la parte alta del cuadro, se las verá de inicio con el australiano Kokkinakis
articles.body: El US Open se congratula del regreso de Carlos Alcaraz a la vez que llora la ausencia por lesión de rodilla de Jannik Sinner. El español y el italiano, que esta campaña sólo han coincidido en el Open de Australia dentro de los cuatro 'Grand Slam', no volverán a verse las caras en uno de ellos hasta la edición 2027 del grande de las Antípodas. Alcaraz, que volvió el martes a la competición en el mixto con Serena Williams 133 días después de la lesión en la muñeca, toparía con Novak Djokovic en unas teóricas semifinales. Se estrenará contra el ruso Roman Safiullin, el 98 del ranking ATP y que ya sabe lo que es ganar al fenómeno de El Palmar. Lo hizo en el Masters 1000 de París, en 2023. Posteriormente, el español igualó el cara a cara en los Juegos Olímpicos de la capital gala. Safiullin, de 29 años, apenas ha ganado tres partidos este curso fuera de los torneos de categoría challenger. Carlitos, como segundo cabeza de serie, no podrá verse las caras con Alexander Zverev, primer favorito, hasta una hipotética final. En el camino del vigente campeón aparecen nombres como Jaime Faria (segunda ronda), Matteo Arnaldi (tercera ronda), Tommy Paul (octavos) y Arthur Fils (cuartos). Zverev intentará demostrar que su título en Roland Garros no fue fruto de la casualidad y de la ausencia en el otro lado de la red de Carlitos, Sinner y Djokovic. El serbio, a sus 39 años, vuelve a estar ante el penúltimo tren para desempolvar su palmarés de grandes. El último fue precisamente hace tres campañas en la Arthur Ashe neoyorquina. Rafa Jódar, de 19 años y decimosegundo cabeza de serie, debuta entre los profesionales después de levantar hace dos campañas el trofeo júnior del Abierto de los Estados Unidos. Su rival en la ronda inicial será el australiano Thanasi Kokkinakis. El primer cabeza de serie en su cuadrante es el noruego Casper Ruud (19), en la tercera ronda. Después tendría a Alex de Miñaur (octavos), Sascha (cuartos) y Taylor Fritz (semifinales). Por lo que hace referencia el resto de miembros de la 'Armada', Carlos Taberner se cruzará con Zizou Bergs (31); Jaume Munar con Terence Atmane; Dani Mérida se las verá con Marton Fucsovics; Martín Landaluce topará con un adversario de la previa; y Pablo Carreño con Jiri Lehecka (18). Podrían unirse Pablo Llamas y Dani Rincón si superan la última ronda de la fase clasificatoria.

articles.title: US Open Tennis Draw 2026 for Novak Djokovic, Carlos Alcaraz as Full Brackets Revealed
articles.summary: The 2026 U.S. Open men's singles final could potentially feature a semifinal showdown between Carlos Alcaraz and Novak Djokovic.
articles.body:
The 2026 U.S. Open men's singles final could potentially feature a semifinal showdown between Carlos Alcaraz and Novak Djokovic.

Alcaraz and Djokovic are featured on the same side of the men's singles draw that was revealed Thursday afternoon.

The women's singles draw placed top-seeded Aryna Sabalenka and Jessica Pegula on track for a potential semifinal matchup of their own.

Here's a look at the full men's and women's brackets now that the draw has been revealed.

Temperatures in Queens will be something to keep an eye on leading into the tournament.

After collapsing during the Cincinnati Open due to what he described as a health issue exacerbated by heat and humidity, Djokovic cut a practice short in the lead-up to the singles draw.

Both Djokovic and Alcaraz are entering the men's singles bracket after elimination in mixed doubles competition earlier this week.

Alcaraz is the defending champion after defeating Jannik Sinner in four sets during the 2025 US Open.

Sinner won't be participating in the 2026 tournament due to a right knee injury, while Alcaraz is making his return from a right wrist injury that sidelined him for four months.

Those injuries could create an opening for the top-seeded participant in the draw, Alexander Zverev, whose 2026 French Open victory made him the first player other than Sinner or Alcaraz to win a major since 2024.

Zverev has reached the U.S. Open semifinals in 2020 and 2021 but has yet to get a chance to play for the tournament title.

In a separate quarter, Felix Auger-Aliassime is looking to take advantage of the opportunity by building on last year's run to the men's single semifinals.

Alex de Minaur (Zverev's quarter) is seeking redemption in the the tournament after falling out of top-four seeding for the event following a fourth-round loss to Arthur Fils at the Cincinnati Masters.

2021 U.S. Open champion Daniil Medvedev (Djokovic's quarter) is also looking for a bounceback tournament after failing to make it past the fourth round at a major this year.

Ben Shelton (Alcaraz's quarter) and Taylor Fritz (Auger-Aliassime's quarter) are each hoping to become the first American man to win the U.S. Open singles title since 2003 .

Shelton is entering the tournament after defending his Canadian Open title earlier this month. Fritz, the 2024 U.S. Open runner-up, most recently made it to the quarterfinals in Cincinnati.

Sabalenka will enter the women's singles field as the favorite to defend her two consecutive U.S. Open victories.

Getting out of her quarter could require overcoming Linda Nosková, who is looking to add another major singles title to her win at the 2026 Wimbledon Championships.

Another one of Sabalenka's top challengers will be Iga Świątek, who defeated Elena Rybakina to win the Canadian Open earlier this month. Świątek may once more need to defeat Rybakina in order to make it out of her quarter.

Coco Gauff is also entering the tournament on a hot streak after recently defeating Pegula to win the Cincinnati Open. She will need to make it out of a quarter featuring 19-year-old Mirra Andreeva in order to earn a shot at a potential final rematch against Pegula.

The main draw of the U.S. Open singles competition begins Aug. 30. The competition leads up to the women's final Sept. 12 and men's final Sept. 13 at Arthur Ashe Stadium.

articles.title: US Open 2026: Carlos Alcaraz faces Roman Safiullin, Novak Djokovic, Aryna Sabalenka & Arthur Fery learn first-round opponents in New York draw
articles.summary: Carlos Alcaraz starts his US Open title defence against Russia's Roman Safiullin in the first serious examination of his fitness following a long-term wrist injury.
articles.body:
Carlos Alcaraz will start his US Open title defence against Russia's Roman Safiullin in the first serious examination of his fitness following a long-term wrist injury.

Second seed Alcaraz, who won the men's title in New York last year, has not played a competitive singles match for more than four months because of inflammation in his playing right wrist.

Despite his lack of action, the 23-year-old Spaniard is still considered by many as the favourite to triumph again - particularly because his great rival Jannik Sinner is not playing due to a knee injury.

The pair may have been a cut above the rest of the tour for the past two seasons, but Alcaraz coming back from a prolonged absence with such a delicate injury and beating the rest of the field - even though he is a generational talent - would be remarkable.

The seven-time major champion missed this season's French Open and Wimbledon as a result of the issue, which did not require surgery, before making his return to court in the US Open mixed doubles alongside Serena Williams earlier this week.

Wearing a long compression sleeve on his right arm, Alcaraz did not look totally convincing in the exhibition-like event. Understandably, he appeared to be holding back on his serve and return as he eased himself back into matchplay.

There is no doubt that a Grand Slam singles bout played over five sets will be another step up physically. Safiullin, with a hefty serve and attacking groundstrokes, is not an ideal opponent to start against.

The 29-year-old Russian, who reached the Wimbledon fourth round last month before falling to Novak Djokovic, is likely to take time away from Alcaraz, test the Spaniard's durability at the baseline and generally make him feel uncomfortable.

Predicting how Slam draws will pan out is always a fool's errand, but if Alcaraz does get past Safiullin and goes as far as the fourth round, there are more potential opponents who appear daunting given the length of his absence.

If you analyse Alcaraz's projected draw by the seedings, he could face rock solid American Tommy Paul or unpredictable Kazak Alexander Bublik in the last 16.

Athletic Frenchman Arthur Fils and huge-serving Ben Shelton are potential quarter-final opponents. Djokovic could lie in wait in the semi-finals.

Nobody outside of Alcaraz and his core team knows how his wrist is likely to stand up to the rigours of playing five-set matches in the heat of a Grand Slam tournament.

A challenging start at Flushing Meadows and a potentially intimidating second week will tell us.

Djokovic's latest quest for a standalone record 25th Grand Slam singles title starts against Argentina's Mariano Navone.

If he gets through that match, the 39-year-old Serb faces a challenging second-round match against either Italy's Matteo Berrettini - who he beat in the 2021 Wimbledon final - or three-time major champion Stan Wawrinka, in what will be the final major of the Swiss player's career after he was given a late wildcard.

Germany's Alexander Zverev, promoted to top seed after Sinner withdrew, faces Italy's Lorenzo Sonego in his opening match.

In the women's draw, defending champion Aryna Sabalenka starts against Colombia's Camila Osorio.

Sabalenka goes into the US Open having topped the WTA rankings for 97 weeks, but knows her place remains under threat from reigning Australian Open champion Elena Rybakina, who has been drawn against American teenage wildcard Thea Frodin.

Two-time champion Venus Williams, 46, has been given a wildcard despite losing all 10 of her matches this season and faces 2020 Australian Open champion Sofia Kenin in the first round.

Mensik & Muchova win US Open mixed doubles title

Wawrinka given late wildcard for US Open farewell

Surprise Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery returns to the Grand Slam stage with a first-round match against Italian 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti.

Fery, 24, produced a career-changing run at the All England Club in July, propelling him into the world's top 40 for the first time and securing his US Open debut in the process.

Fery narrowly missed out on a seeding, which has led to being drawn against Musetti. A quarter-finalist in New York last year, Musetti has recently returned from a thigh injury which ruled him out of the French Open and Wimbledon.

A lot of British attention will be placed on how 37th-ranked Fery fares as he leads a rather sparse contingent in the absence of Jack Draper and Emma Raducanu.

Draper, who reached the 2024 semi-finals, withdrew because of a long-term arm injury, while 2021 champion Raducanu remains sidelined with the shin fracture which also forced her to miss Wimbledon.

British men's number one Cameron Norrie did manage to sneak into the seedings and the 29th seed plays France's Luca van Assche in his opening match.

Jan Choinski is currently the only other Briton in the men's draw after reaching the world's top 100 for the first time in June at the age of 30.

Choinski's reward for earning direct entry into a Grand Slam other than Wimbledon for the first time is a first-round contest with Dutch player Botic van de Zandschulp, who famously beat Alcaraz in the second round of the 2024 US Open.

Katie Boulter is the only Briton guaranteed a place in the women's draw through her ranking and meets American wildcard Carol Young Suh Lee, who is ranked 143rd in the world.

If Boulter wins a Grand Slam match for only the second time this year, the 30-year-old could meet Wimbledon finalist Karolina Muchova in the second round.

Six more Britons - Francesca Jones, Jacob Fearnley, Toby Samuel, Heather Watson, Harriet Dart and Harry Wendelken - aim to reach the main draws by winning their final qualifying matches on Thursday.

articles.summary: Carlos Alcaraz and Novak Djokovic in the same half of the US Open draw as Britain's Arthur Fery is handed a nightmare opening clash; watch the US Open from August 30 live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
Defending champion Alcaraz will open his campaign against Roman Safiullin with a potential semi-final meeting with history-chasing Djokovic.

It will be the Spaniard's first appearance since recovering from a right wrist injury sustained in April.

Djokovic, chasing an elusive 25th Grand Slam title, will face against Argentina's world No 48 Mariano Navone in the first round with the winner to face Matteo Berrettini or Stan Wawrinka, who is playing in his final Grand Slam before retiring.

Wimbledon semi-finalist Fery missed out on a US Open seeding and has paid the price with a daunting first-round meeting against last year's quarter-finalist Musetti.

Speaking on Sky Sports , former British star Naomi Broady gave her reaction to Fery's opening match.

She said: "It is difficult, but you feel with the way Fery has been playing this year, you just don't know what he's capable of.

"Lorenzo is coming back from injury and he didn't play from Rome all the way through and just came back in Canada, so he's going to be rusty. It's going to be an interesting match."

On Alcaraz, she said: "Safiullin could be a tricky draw. The big test for Alcaraz coming back is that it's a best of five sets which is going to be a big test on the wrist and Safiullin hits the ball massive. How's the wrist going to hold up? That's the question mark around Carlos."

World No 33 Cameron Norrie , who reached the semi-finals in Los Cabos and fourth round in Montreal in the build up to the year's final major, takes on a player ranked seven places below him in 22-year-old Belgian-born French player Luca Van Assche.

British No 3 Jan Choinski takes on Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp, ranked world No 71.

In the absence of injured world No 1 Jannik Sinner, Wimbledon finalist Alexander Zverev is the men's top seed at Flushing Meadows and he faces Italy's Lorenzo Sonego.

Defending women's singles champion and world No 1 Aryna Sabalenka, bidding for a third straight US Open title, plays Colombia's Camila Osorio in her first-round match.

Top-ranked Sabalenka has struggled during the North American hard-court swing and could face Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova in the quarter-finals.

Coco Gauff takes on Turkish star Zeynep Sonmez in her first-round match.

Gauff, ​who is seeded fourth and arrives in New York fresh off ​winning the title in Cincinnati, is placed in the bottom half of the draw and could meet Amanda Anisimova ‌in the quarter-finals.

Katie Boulter begins her campaign against American wild card Carol Lee, ranked 143 with Wimbledon finalist and US Open mixed doubles champion Karolina Muchova a potential second-round opponent .

There are six other Brits chasing a main draw spot in qualifying including Fran Jones, Harriet Dart, Heather Watson, Jacob Fearnley, Toby Samuel and Harry Wendelken.

Venus to open against Kenin and not sister Serena!

The draw also delivered one what-could-have-been possibility had Serena Williams decided to play in the singles.

When sister Venus Williams was given a wild card at the age of 46, the USTA initially held one spot, which would have gone to Serena if the six-time champion opted to play for the first time in the main draw since 2022.

But when the 44-year-old decided to only compete in doubles, the USTA awarded that last wild card to American Sofia Kenin, the 2020 Australian Open champion.

On Thursday, Venus Williams and Kenin were drawn to face each other with American Jessica Pegula, who opens against Elena-Gabriela Ruse, a potential second-round opponent.

In some other must-watch ties, Arthur Fils, winner of the Cincinnati Open, faces two-time Grand Slam finalist Stefanos Tsitsipas.

And Stan Wawrinka, the 2016 US Open champion who received a wild card to play in his final Grand Slam tournament before retiring, faces Matteo Berrettini, the 2021 Wimbledon runner-up for the second major running.

"Berrettini might have had the slight advantage on the grass with his massive serve," said Broady. "It's going to be an interesting match."

articles.title: US Open 2026: Why does Venus Williams get so many wildcards?
articles.summary: Venus Williams has not won a singles match in over a year but has received numerous wildcards to compete. The reasons why go beyond just tennis.
articles.body:
Venus Williams has broken many acres of new ground as a tennis player, with five Wimbledon singles titles among her multiple achievements.

The 46-year-old has been playing professionally for nearly 30 years, but her last 14 singles matches have all ended in defeat.

With a world ranking of 611, Williams is reliant on wildcards to compete.

She has had 11 already this season - and the United States Tennis Association (USTA) has offered her a 12th so she can play at the US Open , where she will face fellow Grand Slam champion Sofia Kenin in the first round.

There is a school of thought that argues that, without any wins, it is simply too many, irrespective of her previous achievements.

But there is no limit to the number of wildcards a Grand Slam champion can receive and, for many tournaments, having a Williams sister on site still makes commercial sense.

"I think it's good for tennis to have these generational icons," said Karl Hale, the tournament director who offered Williams a wildcard for this month's WTA 1000 event in Toronto.

"That they are still allocating wildcards for them says something to their intrinsic value to the tournaments."

How to follow US Open on the BBC Published 7 hours ago

Two-time US Open singles champion Williams has not qualified for a Grand Slam by ranking since Wimbledon 2021, which is also where she recorded her most recent singles win at a major.

She has been competitive in her past two Slam singles matches, pushing 11th seed Karolina Muchova to three sets in New York last year, and narrowly losing in three sets to Olga Danilovic at January's Australian Open.

Williams was also a doubles quarter-finalist at last year's US Open, but the defeat by qualifier Emiliana Arango in Cincinnati this month was her 18th loss in 19 singles matches. The only bright spot has been a win over Peyton Stearns in Washington last July.

And yet this year alone tournament directors in New Zealand, Australia, Spain, Germany and Canada - as well as the United States - have wanted Williams at their events.

Eight of the 128 spots in a Grand Slam singles draw are assigned to wildcards, and usually between four and eight at WTA and ATP events depending on the size of the field.

"The way we looked at Venus is that her legacy is phenomenal," Hale told BBC Sport.

"She's done so much for the sport and is really popular here in Toronto and our markets specifically - so we thought it was really good to announce it early that we have a Williams sister coming."

Hale says the media interest was significant, which he believes in turn drives ticket sales.

"The wildcards always play first-round matches, and with the bigger draw [size] now, it adds more notable names and stars for the beginning of the tournament," he said.

"Venus played opening day. She kicked off our tournament, so it added a lot of value."

'You never want a player you're unsure of'

Most tournaments will prioritise their own national players for wildcards, but they are also given to names who are likely to add commercial value to the event.

There are also what Hale calls 'trades' with other national federations or agencies like IMG, which manages players and until recently also owned the Miami and Madrid Opens.

The most obvious example of a 'trade' is the reciprocal wildcard agreement between the USTA, Tennis Australia and the French Tennis Federation. Each of these Grand Slam nations offers a men's and a women's wildcard to the others, knowing two of their players will benefit when it is their counterparts' turn to host.

One sporting event which has reduced the opportunity for past champions to return is the Open Golf Championship.

Twenty years ago, any champions under 65 could play whenever they wished. Now, winners only get the chance to return until they are 55, which could open up the odd place in the field to younger, more highly ranked professionals.

Golfers can be competitive for much longer, but there are no limits in tennis. Martina Navratilova was given a wildcard for both the 2004 French Open and Wimbledon - and won a round on the grass - when she made a comeback aged 47.

"You never want to put a player out there that you are unsure about," said Hale, who believes Williams is still capable of winning matches.

"Venus lost 6-4 6-1 to Kamilla Rakhimova, and the first set was really competitive. She's still competitive, but just not winning these matches."

So should there be a limit; a moment when a tournament director offers the spot to a more highly ranked player trying to advance their career?

"When the time comes that Venus is not competitive in sets, then I think she will make that call," Hale responded.

"Venus and Serena have done so much for women's tennis and the sport that they should be able to play as long as they want.

"I'm very happy they are continuing and they make their decision when they are ready, or each tournament makes their decision when they are ready."

British number one Katie Boulter put it a similar way after she partnered the "absolute icon" in the Madrid doubles in April.

"Venus has given so much to our sport that she deserves to get what she needs back," she said then.

"We have to be grateful that she is still out there, doing the best she can."

articles.title: Elise Mertens Set to Face Nikola Bartunkova in WTA Monterrey Semifinals
articles.summary: The early round action at WTA Monterrey, the Abierto GNP Seguros has lead to a pair of compelling semifinals on Friday. Diane Parry from France will take on...
articles.body:
The early round action at WTA Monterrey, the Abierto GNP Seguros has lead to a pair of compelling semifinals on Friday. Diane Parry from France will take on #5 seed Ann Li, while the rising Nikola Bartunkova takes on the tournament favorite, Elise Mertens.

Elise Mertens into WTA Monterrey Semifinals

The late-night quarterfinal at WTA Monterrey saw Mertens power past Yuliia Starodubtseva 6-1 6-4, as she dominated on her service games and didn't face a single break point. Mertens needed three sets to get past Panna Udvardy in the previous round, similarly performing better on serve.

Mertens, 30, is nearing her second consecutive season of 30+ match wins and has put together her best result this week since the quarterfinals at Wimbledon. With the US Open draw already made, Mertens is set to face Kaitlin Quevedo in the first round, and could face Naomi Osaka in round 3.

Bartunkova, Li, and Parry Complete Semifinal Lineup in Monterrey

The semifinal field at WTA Monterrey was completed on Thursday. Diane Parry scored a slight upset over Clara Tauson 6-3 7-5, converting all of her break point chances in the match. Parry has a chance to reach a career high ranking this week inside the top 50. Her semifinal opponent is Ann Li from the United States, Li, 26, finally advanced her record above 500 this season by dispatching her fellow American Alycia Parks 6-2 6-3. Li only needed two wins to reach the semis this week as she was granted a walkover in the round of 16. It's her best result since Strasbourg on clay in May, which also happened a week before a Grand Slam. Both sets of semifinals are matchups where there is h2h history.

20-year-old Nikola Bartunkova will be the opponent for the tactically minded Mertens. She's battled past consecutive three setters this week, defeating En Shuo Liang and qualifier Darja Vidmanova to reach the semifinals. This is her first year fully active on the WTA Tour and her best WTA level result. She reached the final of the Birmingham 125 in June.

Both of Bartunkova's WTA semifinals have come in Mexico, as she was a standout in Guadalajara in 2025. With that, the stage is set for three more thrilling singles matches in Monterrey, with the final scheduled for Saturday.

articles.title: Winston-Salem Open: Arthur Fery beats Aleksandar Kovacevic to reach semi-finals
articles.summary: Britain's Arthur Fery comes from a set down to beat Aleksandar Kovacevic and book his place in the semi-finals of the Winston-Salem Open.
articles.body:
Britain's Arthur Fery came from a set down to beat Aleksandar Kovacevic and book his place in the semi-finals of the Winston-Salem Open.

Fourth seed Fery, who won five games in a row from 5-5 in the second set, claimed a 3-6 7-5 6-3 victory in Thursday's last-eight match in North Carolina.

After breaking Kovacevic to take the second set, Fery opened up a 3-0 lead in the third, serving out to clinch his first semi-final appearance since Wimbledon in July.

The 24-year-old will face James Duckworth, who he beat in Cincinnati earlier this month, in the last four, after the Australian defeated Hungarian 15th seed Fabian Marozsan 6-7 (4-7) 6-2 6-4.

Fery's surprise run to the Wimbledon semi-finals this summer lifted him into the top 40 in the world rankings - he is now 37th - and with it a place in the US Open for the first time.

He just missed out on being seeded for the final Grand Slam of the year at Flushing Meadows in New York so has been drawn against 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti in the opening round.

articles.summary: Carlos Alcaraz and Aryna Sabalenka look to defend their titles as the year’s final Grand Slam begins on Sunday.
articles.body:
The season of Honey Deuce cocktails at Flushing Meadows is upon us as the 2026 US Open main draw gets under way in New York this Sunday.

This year’s fourth and final Grand Slam will feature some of the biggest names in tennis and breakout players on the up and up, although there will also be some notable injured absentees.

The mixed doubles title has already been claimed by Czech pair Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik on Wednesday night after defeating Switzerland’s Belinda Bencic and Italy’s Flavio Cobolli.

Here’s everything you need to know about the US Open main draw:

All the main draw action from August 30 until September 13 is at the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in Flushing Meadows, just outside New York City.

The men’s and women’s quarterfinals begin on September 8 , followed by:

Women’s singles semifinals: September 10

Top-ranked Jannik Sinner withdraws: The World number one said he was “very sad and disappointed” to withdraw from after being unable to recover from a right knee injury that has sidelined him since winning the Wimbledon title. The Italian pulled out of hard-court tournaments in Montreal and Cincinnati that serve as a warm-up for the US Open.

Carlos Alcaraz back in action: The Spaniard will look to defend his title after a four-month hiatus from tennis due to a wrist injury, but Sinner’s absence means the crowd will not see the beloved “Sincaraz” rivalry this time.

Serena Williams, Alcaraz pair up for iconic mixed doubles duo: Two generational greats teamed up for this year’s mixed doubles, although their star power faded as they fell to Cobolli and Bencic in the quarterfinal.

Serena and Venus Williams receive doubles wildcard: The 23-time Grand Slam champion received a women’s doubles wildcard alongside older sister Venus. They have played together at the US Open nine times, winning in 1999 and 2009. Venus also received a wildcard for the women’s singles.

2016 champion Stan Wawrinka handed last-minute wildcard: The former world number three was left off the initial list of wildcard entries in his farewell season, but was handed the entry on Wednesday after several days of outcry from fans over his exclusion.

Teen sensation Moise Kouame makes US Open debut: The 17-year-old made history at this year’s French Open when he became the youngest male Grand Slam winner in 17 years. However, the Frenchman’s US Open debut ended in the qualifying round after defeat to Nishesh Basavareddy of the US.

Novak Djokovic continues pursuit of elusive 25th slam: The world number five Djokovic has been in relentless pursuit of a record 25th Slam title since winning his 24th at the US Open in 2023. The Serbian’s ambition has repeatedly been tested by age as the 39-year-old struggled with stifling humidity at this month’s Cincinnati Open. Still, he reached the Australian Open final this year as well as the Wimbledon semifinal.

No. The 45-year-old Swiss icon categorically ruled out a Williams-esque return.

His brief on-court appearance in New York this week was for primetime exhibition matches ahead of a trip to Newport, Rhode Island to be enshrined in the International Tennis Hall of Fame on Saturday.

With Sinner out of contention, Alcaraz has a clear shot at his title defence for a third US Open win.

Wimbledon champion and top seed Alexander Zverev will also be looking to carry momentum from his maiden Slam win in June, although the German was knocked out in the fourth round at last week’s Cincinnati Open.

Arthur Fils, seeded 23rd, could be a surprise contender in the final four after the Frenchman defeated American Frances Tiafoe to clinch his maiden Masters 1000 title in Cincinnati last week.

Over on the women’s side, Gauff will look to defeat top-ranked Sabalenka for a repeat of her maiden US Open title in 2023, although the Belarusian will be eyeing a third consecutive win in New York.

That being said, the 28-year-old has faltered this season after a fourth round defeat in Cincinnati , the Toronto Masters , Wimbledon and a quarterfinal exit at Roland Garros .

World number two Rybakina is hot on Sabalenka’s heels for the top spot with 8,141 points to Sabalenka’s 8,575.

At 32, Jessica Pegula is the oldest top 10 player, but has been a finalist and semifinalist in the past two years and will look to continue that on home soil this year too.

Russian teenager Andreeva bagged her maiden Slam title at the French Open this summer and sits at a career-high world number five, although a fourth round appearance in New York will be her deepest at the US Open.

Alex Eala of the Philippines will be a force to watch after the 21-year-old found her breakthrough with a maiden WTA title this month at the Washington Open.

She received a wildcard for the US Open mixed doubles with Auger-Aliassime, although the duo fell in the first round to husband-and-wife duo of Gael Monfils and Svitolina.

Eala will headline the Stars of the Open exhibition event at Arthur Ashe on Thursday alongside young players Joao Fonseca, Iva Jovic and Learner Tien.

A record $108m prize pot is up for grabs this time:

Winner: $5.5m Finalist: $2.8m Semi-finalist: $1.45m Quarter-finalist: $780,000 Round of 16: $480,000 Round of 32: $290,000 Round of 64: $190,000 Round of 128: $140,000 Qualifying Round of 32: $66,000 Qualifying Round of 64: $48,000 Qualifying Round of 128: $32,000

Who are some notable absences this year?

Alongside Sinner, Brazil’s Fonseca (ATP 26th ranking) and Briton Jack Draper (ATP 141st ranking) will be absent from the men’s side.

Emma Raducanu of Britain, world number 15 Victoria Mboko of Canada and Hailey Baptiste of the US, ranked 34rd, are other big names who won’t be in action.

articles.title: Roger Federer Speaks Out Ahead of 2026 Tennis Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony
articles.summary: On the eve of his formal induction into the Tennis Hall of Fame, Roger Federer reflected back on his legendary career.
articles.body:
On the eve of his formal induction into the Tennis Hall of Fame, Roger Federer reflected back on his legendary career.

Federer told reporters prior to being enshrined in the Hall of Fame on Saturday that retirement has afforded him the chance to think about how he impacted the sport beyond his accomplishments on the court:

"I think when you retire, I think I said it before, that there was a lot of talk also about maybe my personality and what I brought to the game overall when I wasn't on court, which I was a little surprised. I thought it was about, in the moment, forehands and backhands and saving break points and victories and all that stuff. But actually it becomes a little bit, not irrelevant eventually, but it's about what were you remembered for, how did you behave in the locker rooms or in the corridors or maybe with the media, or with the tournament directors, the ball kids."

In the four years since officially retiring from competition, Federer admitted he "dearly" misses playing and that he still hears from fans who tell him how much they wish he was still able to compete.

"For me, if I look back, that's kind of what I'm very happy about, that I went through 25 years on tour, and actually felt like I made a lot of friends and a lot of people miss me," Federer said. "Same with fans. They come up to me and say, 'What a shame you're not playing anymore.' Then I get a flashback saying it was an amazing time, and I say it every time. I loved it, and it's a shame I can't be on the tour anymore. But it was a great, great time and I miss it dearly."

Federer hasn't completely left his playing days behind. He recently returned to the court at Arthur Ashe Stadium for an exhibition match against Andy Roddick.

Federer also teamed up with John McEnroe against Roddick and Andre Agassi.

The 45-year-old won both matches, defeating Roddick 6-3 in the singles competition and a 7-5 win with McEnroe over Roddick and Agassi in the doubles event.

Federer won 103 singles titles during his 24-year playing career, including 20 Grand Slam championships. He also won two Olympic medals, including gold in doubles with Stan Wawrinka at the 2008 Games.

The International Tennis Hall of Fame announced in November 2025 that Federer and journalist/sportscaster Mary Carillo were named to the Hall as part of the Class of 2026.

Federer will formally be enshrined during a ceremony on Saturday at 6:30 p.m. ET.

articles.summary: Según Forbes, el español es el segundo jugador mejor pagado del año con 53,7 millones de dólares en una lista en la que ocho de los 10 tenistas han ingresado más fuera de la pista que dentro de ella
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz, a pesar de llevar cuatro meses fuera de las pistas, vuelve a estar entre los tenistas mejor pagados del año según la revista Forbes. El murciano marca unos ingresos aproximados de 53,7 millones de dólares en una lista en la que Jannik Sinner ha relevado al español, líder en 2025, y por primera vez es el jugador con más ganancias de los últimos 12 meses con 58 millones. Aunque Alcaraz es el tenista masculino que más genera fuera de la pista. De los 53,7 millones de dólares que ha ingresado el fenómeno de El Palmar, 38 millones son por contratos publicitarios. En este aspecto, supera al italiano por tres millones. Nike, Babolat, Itaú, Isdin, Rolex, El Pozo, Louis Vuitton, BMW, Infosys y Evian son algunas de las marcas que respaldan la carrera del campeón de siete Grand Slam, que estará muy presente durante estas semanas en la publicidad de las calles de Nueva York. En cambio, la ventaja de Sinner va más por lo que ha logrado en la pista. En premios es el líder absoluto con un techo de 23 millones de dólares, 8,7 millones más que el español (15,7 millones). Eso sí, el de San Cándido ha contado con cuatro meses más de competición debido a la lesión de muñeca que ha dejado fuera de la competición por cuatro meses al español. La tenista estadounidense es la tercera del ranking con 40,1 millones de dólares ingresados en 2026, de los cuales 40 millones son generados fuera de la pista. Es embajadora de su empresa, Serena Ventures, aparte de su idilio de 23 años con Nike. Tan solo 100.000 dólares son de premios económicos. Serena decidió regresar al deporte de su vida tras cuatro años de "retiro". En este tiempo ha disputado Wimbledon, la modalidad de dobles en Cincinnati y el dobles mixto junto a Alcaraz. De los 10 tenistas de la lista, solo dos cuentan con más ganancias por premios económicos que por publicidad, Alexander Zverev (segunda aparición) y Elena Rybakina. El alemán, número dos mundial y vigente campeón de Roland Garros, tiene unos ingresos aproximados de 13,7 millones de dólares por su tenis, mientras que los cinco millones restantes, son de todo lo que hay fuera del deporte. Más de lo mismo con la kazaja, que sobre la pista ha sumado 11,4 millones, mientras que seis han sido fuera de ella.

articles.title: US Open 2026: The Honey Deuce is ready to take on all cocktail challengers. More than 700,000 were served last year, and, 'We aim to break that record'
articles.summary: This year marks the 20th Open since Grey Goose first introduced the iconic Honey Deuce cocktail to the world.
articles.body:
The 2026 US Open marks a milestone not just for the fast-paced action on the courts across the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in Flushing, Queens, but for the hundreds of thousands of fans who can't wait to get their hands on one specific sweet, boozy treat.

This year marks the 20th Open since Grey Goose first introduced the iconic Honey Deuce cocktail to the world, and the concoction made of vodka, lemonade and raspberry liqueur poured into a commemorative cup and garnished with a skewer of three green "tennis" melon balls is more popular than ever. As more than 1.14 million fans saw tennis' final Grand Slam of the year live in 2025, the USTA said that a record 738,459 honey deuces were sold during the Open's three weeks last year. That means the Open brought in nearly $17 million in revenue from the $23 beverage.

"This year, we aim to break that record," Chris Studley, the managing director of event services for the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, told Yahoo Sports.

One bartender I spoke with last year said he was whipping up several hundred Honey Deuces on a given day. Studley said that the most Honey Deuces sold on a single day in 2025 was nearly 60,000. And since it will remain the same price for the third straight year, servers will remain busy all day, every day.

But what makes this sweet sensation the most recognizable cocktail in all of sports, surpassing the once powerful Kentucky Derby Mint Julep?

"The Honey Deuce isn't just a refreshing cocktail, it's an anchor of the US Open experience," Studley said. "It's light, fun, and looks great in the commemorative cup. And for many fans, it's a tradition to enjoy a Honey Deuce while walking the grounds and watching some of the world's best tennis. It perfectly captures the electric energy of late summer in New York."

Every year, there are new drink offerings that are touted as rivals to the Honey Deuce. The Ace Paloma, a Dobel tequila cocktail mixed with grapefruit soda and a squeeze of lime, and the Aperol Spritz both had their moments in 2025. But this year, Moët is entering the chat in a major way.

The Open's official champagne sponsor came up with the Moët Serve, champagne served over ice with three lemon wheels in a glass that's made to look like an old-school plastic tennis ball canister. The $20 beverage will be sold only at the American Express Card Member Lounge and the luxury Club de Tennis Bar. The collaboration demonstrates how AmEx works with other premium partners to elevate the Open experience for its card members, American Express said.

The Serve has the Instagrammable sex appeal, with the bubbly combined with the tennis-themed vessel, to become one of the viral sensations of the tournament. But will it have enough staying power to challenge the mighty Honey Deuce for US Open supremacy? It would have to be offered in more locations in the future to truly be a contender, but we'll see over the next few weeks if the Serve's scarcity and exclusivity works in its favor.

On the food side, Studley said a few standouts have emerged early that could be this year's smash hit of Cocodaq's $100 chicken nugget box that came with a can of caviar on the side. Salt Hank's famous French Dip sandwich arrives at the US Open for the first time this year, as social media star Henry Laporte imports the item that has lines around the block of his West Village storefront every day. Chef Enrique Olvera's Cosme brings its showstopping duck carnitas to Queens this year for their debut, while Israeli fast-casual chain Miznon brings its crowd-pleasing green beans to the party.

And while food offerings will come and go each year at the Open, no food or beverage item in any sporting event has had as much fanfare or staying power over the past two decades as the Honey Deuce. While drinks like the Moët Serve will try their best, it seems like the Honey Deuce is more secure on its end-of-summer throne than ever before as the signature beverage for tennis' signature event.

articles.title: No Jannik Sinner ... a rusty Carlos Alcaraz ... and a US Open that could get wild
articles.summary: With the Sinner-Alcaraz rivalry on hold, this US Open is wide open.
articles.body:
When the US Open ended a year ago, all the evidence pointed to Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner continuing to meet in every major final as far as the eye could see.

Not only had they battled for the title in Paris, London and New York, the gap between them and the rest of the field seemed to only be growing. It was a rivalry in full bloom and in many ways a race to history, reminiscent of the early dominance that Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal once shared.

But as another US Open begins Sunday, there is only one thing we know for sure: Alcaraz and Sinner will end 2026 without meeting in any of the Grand Slams.

Though Alcaraz has made it to New York after missing 4 1/2 months with a wrist injury, Sinner has not played since winning Wimbledon and is out with a knee issue. A weird, injury-plagued year in men's tennis will end weirdly and injury-plagued at the US Open.

Should Alcaraz be considered the favorite to win his eighth major? Under normal circumstances, he's that much better than the rest of the field, but these are not normal circumstances.

Alcaraz has been ramping up for several weeks back home in Spain, but the decision to come back without a warmup tournament carries some risk and uncertainty. If Alcaraz had been ready to play at the Masters 1000 event in Cincinnati, he would have. Instead, he'll dive into a best-of-five format having not played since the Monte Carlo final on April 12.

How will the wrist hold up? How much competitive rust will he need to shake off? Alcaraz will probably be fine if he can get through the first week, but his team probably wasn't thrilled to see Roman Safiullin pop up as a first-round opponent. There are a lot of players in the draw that don't have the firepower to beat Alcaraz under any circumstances. Safiullin is one who does if you catch him on the wrong day.

It sets up a US Open, at least in theory, that could resemble the French Open from just a few months ago where Alcaraz was rehabbing back home and Sinner suffered some kind of heat reaction when he was up two sets to love against Juan Manuel Cerundolo, collapsing to a second-round defeat.

What happened after that? Almost complete chaos. As players realized the opportunity in front of them, there were fascinating matches unfolding on a daily basis. There was also a lot of anxiety and outright choking until finally Alexander Zverev emerged with his long-awaited first major, outlasting Flavio Cobolli in five sets.

As for Zverev, who inherited the No. 1 seed for the tournament but has never been ranked No. 1 in the world? He doesn't look like a great pick either.

Though he played excellent tennis at Wimbledon to reach his first final there, Zverev's subsequent hard court results have been scratchy, losing early in both Montreal and Cincinnati. He's also not played very well in general in New York over the last few years. Zverev has talked in the past about struggling to control the US Open's Wilson brand ball, which feels a bit lighter on the racket and flies through the air quicker than other balls that are used at different tournaments.

It's hard to have much confidence in 39-year old Novak Djokovic either. Since losing to Sinner in the Wimbledon semifinals, he's played just one match: A three-set loss to 42nd-ranked Thiago Agustin Tirante in Cincinnati in which he once against struggled with the heat, at one point keeling over and vomiting.

Though the weather forecast for the US Open looks pretty mild, Djokovic has not given much evidence over the last couple years that he can hold up enough physically to withstand seven matches in the best-of-five format. His quest for a 25th major continues, but it would be a real surprise at this point.

That brings us to the elephant in the room: The American players.

It's a tired storyline by now, but it's been the storyline for 23 straight years since Andy Roddick's US Open title. When is an American going to win a major again?

The usual suspects should all be feeling a lot of confidence, particularly this year given their recent hard court form, their track record at the US Open and the discombobulated state of the field. Taylor Fritz, who reached the finals two years ago, won Washington. Ben Shelton, a semifinalist in 2023, won Canada for the second straight year. Frances Tiafoe, twice a semifinalist, got his game going in Cincinnati and reached the final.

They will have the crowds behind them. They will also carry the most pressure of anyone in the field. Until one of them does it, skepticism is warranted.

This also feels like the kind of tournament that could mint tennis' next superstar. Injuries have slowed the progress of 22-year old Frenchman Arthur Fils, but he is an electric performer, has won 32 of 42 matches on the year and just bagged his first Masters 1000 title in Cincinnati. Rafael Jodar, the 19-year old Spaniard, has beaten Fils twice this summer and it seems to be a matter of when, not if, he's going to regularly challenge for Slam titles.

Make no mistake, this US Open would be better if Sinner and Alcaraz were in the field. It's a real bummer that after some of the historically great battles they've had on the biggest stages, only one of them will even play the final three majors of the year.

Let's hope for better luck in 2027. But in the meantime, let's enjoy a US Open that will either give us another chapter in the Alcaraz legend or a result that few of us could have seen coming.

articles.standfirst: El murciano habla ante los medios por primera vez desde su lesión en Barcelona y afirma "estar preparado" para el reto
articles.summary: El murciano habla ante los medios por primera vez
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz habló delante de los medios en el 'media day' del US Open por primera vez desde que se lesionara de la muñeca derecha en el Barcelona Open Banc Sabadell ante el finlandés Otto Virtanen. Lo que le ha obligado a perderse grandes citas del calendario como Roland Garros, Wimbledon y los Masters 1000 de Madrid, Roma, Canadá y Cincinnati. El murciano dará comienzo a su camino hacia la defensa del título el lunes 31 de agosto ante el ruso Roman Safiullin, número 98 del ranking ATP. Alcaraz aseguró que la incertidumbre de su lesión fue lo más difícil de llevar mentalmente: "En cuanto empecé a entrenar un poco, aunque no sabía cuándo iba a poder hacerlo, surgieron pensamientos realmente difíciles de gestionar. No sabía si estaría listo para Cincinnati o el US Open, o si me perdería toda la gira americana. Lidiar con esos pensamientos fue muy complicado. Pero finalmente aquí estamos. Mi objetivo era intentar estar sano lo antes posible y no perder más competiciones. Así que diría que esos pensamientos intrusivos fueron la parte más difícil de todo este proceso", anotó el de El Palmar. "Los primeros meses fueron algo difíciles para mí porque no podía hacer nada con el brazo derecho. Fue duro, pero al mismo tiempo disfruté del tiempo con mi familia y mis amigos, estando en casa", añadió en relación a los primeros meses de su lesión. Pese a la gravedad de la lesión y el dolor, ha dejado claro claro que no ha modificado su estilo de juego para proteger la articulación: "He estado haciendo las mismas cosas. No he cambiado nada en cuanto a la técnica ni a mis movimientos ni a la forma en la que voy a jugar. Simplemente quería sentir que iba a ser yo mismo. Si hubiera sentido que tenía que cambiar algo para volver aquí, no podría estar aquí. Para mí lo más importante es mantener mi identidad". El tema de su manera de jugar lo cerró con una frase al más puro estilo Alcaraz: "Vamos a ver al Carlitos de la manera que siempre ha jugado". "Sabía que venir aquí, al US Open, siendo un torneo al mejor de cinco sets y siendo el primero después de tanto tiempo, iba a ser un desafío enorme. Probablemente, en términos de preparación, no era el momento ideal. Pero mi equipo y yo creemos que estoy preparado. Creo que no hay mejor torneo que el US Open para regresar, y sentir el cariño de la gente de aquí", declaraba el número tres del ranking ATP, que ya tiene ganas de saltar a la Arthur Ashe. También mencionó a Rafa Nadal y Roger Federer como ejemplo de inspiración de vuelta de una lesión: "Federer, Nadal, mucha gente ha demostrado que se puede ganar un Grand Slam después de haber estado lesionado mucho tiempo". Agradeció la semana de entrenamientos con el danés (lesionado del tendón de Aquiles) en la Real Sociedad Club de Campo de Murcia: "Fue una semana muy importante para mí. Tengo que agradecer a Holger que viniera a entrenar conmigo. Está en muy buena forma. Obviamente todavía necesita más rehabilitación, pero me ayudó mucho a darme cuenta de que estoy preparado para volver aquí y competir. Es bienvenido allí siempre que lo necesite. Me alegró mucho verlo de nuevo en pista". Y dejó un espacio para dedicarle unas palabras a su máximo rival y gran amigo Jannik Sinner debido a su reciente baja del último grande del año: "Creo que todos sentimos lo mismo cuando alguien como Jannik se pierde este torneo. No vamos a vernos durante unos seis o siete meses. Es una situación bastante rara, para ser sincero. Le deseo todo lo mejor. Espero que tenga una gran recuperación y que vuelva a las pistas en su máximo nivel", cerró Carlos Alcaraz.

articles.title: Coco Gauff Defends Mom's Statement on Rejecting US Open Ticket Requests, 'Honestly, It Was Needed'
articles.summary: American tennis star Coco Gauff supported her mother's decision to share a social media post pushing back against requests for guest tickets to the 2026 U.S. Open.
articles.body:
American tennis star Coco Gauff supported her mother's decision to share a social media post pushing back against requests for guest tickets to the 2026 U.S. Open.

Gauff told reporters she was initially surprised by her mother's Instagram post but ultimately understood her reasoning.

"Honestly, it was needed, and it was directed toward a few family and friends," Gauff said Friday.

"To be honest, yeah, people come out of the woodwork. You haven't spoken to someone for years, they don't say 'Congrats' or 'Happy birthday' or nothing, and then they're like, 'Oh, I'm in New York, can I have eight tickets to your match in your box please?'"

Candi Gauff posted what she called a "blunt, but necessary statement" in the caption to an Aug. 27 post featuring Gauff holding the Cincinnati Open trophy.

"Unfortunately, I will not be able to hook you up with a ticket. Please make arrangements to purchase a ticket," Gauff's mother wrote. "Side note, never ask for more than 2 tickets."

Gauff said Friday she feels the U.S. Open and Wimbledon are the two tournaments during which her parents field the most requests for guest tickets.

Gauff, who climbed to No. 4 in the WTA rankings after her win in Cincinnati, is seeded fourth in this year's women's singles tournament.

She is currently preparing for a first-round matchup with Zeynep Sönmez, the world No. 52 who upset Ekaterina Alexandrova in the first round of the 2026 Australian Open. Gauff and Sönmez will face off at Arthur Ashe Stadium this Sunday.

articles.title: US Open 2026: Katie Boulter won't repeat Andy Murray wedding ring mistake as she prepares for final major of season
articles.summary: Andy Murray has long been a guiding figure for British tennis, but newly-married Katie Boulter will not be following his lead when it comes to keeping her wedding ring safe as she prepares for the US Open.
articles.body:
Andy Murray has long been a guiding figure for British tennis, but newly-married Katie Boulter will not be following his lead when it comes to keeping her wedding ring safe.

Three-time Grand Slam champion Murray, who married wife Kim in 2015, famously briefly lost his wedding band after playing with it tied to his shoe laces.

Murray had left his trainers - with the ring still attached - under a car to dry out after a practice session in California in 2021, and after discovering they were missing the next day, was eventually reunited with both after putting out an appeal for their return.

Boulter, who married Australia's world number seven Alex de Minaur this summer, said she will not be making the same mistake.

"I learned from Andy. I'm not going to do that," the 30-year-old said. "I don't wear it. Not during matches."

Boulter and De Minaur tied the knot at a small, private ceremony in England before holding a bigger celebration in Tuscany, Italy, in July.

Speaking to BBC Sport, Boulter said: "One was in the UK for my nearest and dearest. It was like eight people - very, very small, very much for my grandpa.

"It was a huge contrast to the Italian wedding, which had all of our closest people, all of our friends, and was a little bit more of a party and a lot of fun."

When it came to De Minaur's speech, however, Boulter admitted she was "sceptical".

"I hadn't seen him do any preparation for the speech at all. And he was like, 'I'm just going to wing it. It's fine. How hard can it be?'," she said.

"He was amazing. He was so, good. I was crying the whole time. I think I permanently cried for like three hours straight during all the speeches."

Since their wedding, the world number 60 has wasted no time in throwing herself back into tennis before the US Open, which gets under way on Sunday.

"I actually just chose to go straight back into the conditions, go into the deep end and see what we've got," said Boulter, who lost in the first round in Washington and Toronto before suffering a second-round exit in Cincinnati.

"I do think the conditions in the States are very different from the UK. I think you can't really replicate them.

"So I felt like I'd be a little underprepared coming to the US and just getting used to the conditions again would have been quite difficult."

Boulter's US Open begins with a first-round encounter against American wildcard Carol Young Suh Lee, who is ranked 143rd in the world.

Who plays who in the US Open first round?

Injury uncertainty led to 'intrusive thoughts' for Alcaraz

Record number of British players qualify for main draw at US Open

A record four British players have made it through qualifying to reach the main draw at the US Open.

Fran Jones, Harriet Dart and Harry Wendelken all won their third and final qualifying matches on Friday, while Toby Samuel advanced on Thursday after his opponent, Chile's Cristian Garin, retired during a lengthy rain delay.

It is the first time that four British players have progressed from qualifying at an overseas Grand Slam since the Australian Open of 1988.

Jacob Fearnley lost to Austria's Jurij Rodionov in a rain-disrupted match that stretched across Thursday and Friday, but the 25-year-old will play Spain's Martin Landaluce in the first round after securing a main draw spot as a lucky loser.

The five Britons will join compatriots Arthur Fery, Cameron Norrie, Jan Choinski and Boulter in the main draws.

Wendelken earned his first appearance in the main draw at an overseas Grand Slam as he fought back to beat Lithuania's Vilius Gaubas 6-7 (3-7) 7-6 (7-5) 7-6 (10-5).

He will face Italian 22nd seed Luciano Darderi in the first round, while Samuel is up against the Czech Republic's Tomas Machac.

Jones, meanwhile, claimed a straightforward 6-4 6-1 win over Taiwan's Joanna Garland to qualify for a second successive year and set up a first-round meeting with Poland's Magda Linette

Meanwhile, Heather Watson missed out on her first US Open singles main-draw appearance in five years as Dart fought back from a set and a break down to win 2-6 6-4 6-1.

"It's never easy playing against a friend and Heather is such an a great player and has so much experience," Dart told BBC Sport.

"It showed for an hour and a half, I was really behind and she was playing some really good tennis. In the end I was able to stick to it somehow and find a way and turn it in my favour."

Dart, who has reached the second round in her last two main draw appearances at Flushing Meadows, will play American Peyton Stearns in the first round.

articles.title: US Open 2026: Carlos Alcaraz had 'intrusive thoughts' over when he would return from wrist injury
articles.summary: Seven-time major champion Carlos Alcaraz says not knowing when he would be able to return from a wrist injury was most challenging part of his long absence.
articles.body:
Seven-time major champion Carlos Alcaraz says dealing with "intrusive thoughts" over when he would be able to return from his wrist injury was the most challenging part of his long absence.

Spain's Alcaraz, 23, has not played a singles match since mid-April but says he feels "great" as he prepares to make his comeback at the US Open, which begins in New York on Sunday.

Alcaraz, who beat rival Jannik Sinner in last year's final at Flushing Meadows, starts his title defence against powerful Russian Roman Safiullin in a contest which is likely to examine his lack of competitive action.

"Once I started to practice a little bit but didn't know when I'm going to [return], those thoughts were really difficult to deal with," said Alcaraz.

"I didn't know if I was going to be ready for Cincinnati, for the US Open, or [if] I'm going to miss the whole American swing.

"That was really difficult to deal with, but finally here we are. Those intrusive thoughts were the most difficult things to deal with in this process."

Why tough US Open draw will be true test of Alcaraz's fitness

How to follow US Open on the BBC Published 8 hours ago

Alcaraz made his return to a match court at the US Open earlier this week, when he played alongside 23-time Grand Slam singles champion Serena Williams in the mixed doubles event.

Alcaraz, who won the New York title in 2022 and 2025, continues to wear a compression sleeve on his playing arm in a bid to protect his wrist.

Wrist injuries are notoriously problematic for tennis players - and taking a gamble when an issue arises in this delicate area can be very costly.

Alcaraz has needed to show patience as he dealt with what is thought to be tenosynovitis, where the sheath that protects the tendon on the inside of the wrist becomes inflamed.

Alcaraz generates huge amounts of power through his forehand, which puts a lot of load through the joint of his playing wrist.

But speaking on Friday, he insists he feels mentally ready to compete in five-set matches at the highest level.

"It's really challenging. Probably, you know, in terms of preparation and everything, it is not the best time," said Alcaraz, who will be seeded second at the tournament despite his extended lay-off.

"But we, my team and me, believe that I'm ready."

He added: "I've got to trust my team, I've got to trust my people that tell me it's going be fine.

"I just have to go 100%, and right now I think with the practices I have done so far, it's been all good.

"I'm trying to stay away from any fear and I'm playing normal."

articles.title: US Open: Carlos Alcaraz admits he needs competition as he prepares for his title defence after wrist injury
articles.summary: Carlos Alcaraz insists he will not be holding back as he bids to defend his US Open title; watch the US Open from August 30 live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
Carlos Alcaraz says he is "feeling great" as he prepares for his US Open defence in what will be the Spaniard's first appearance since recovering from a right wrist injury sustained in April.

Alcaraz's long absence has clouded his prospects, but the seven-time Grand Slam champion has built a reputation for producing his best tennis on the grandest stages and cannot ‌be discounted despite the uncertainty surrounding his return.

He will launch his title defence against Russia's Roman Safiullin following a quick tune-up alongside Serena Williams in the mixed doubles.

"I'm feeling very good, and I think that injury helped me a lot to understand that right now, everything is in my head. I have to trust my team, trust the people who tell me that everything is going to be fine," said the 23-year-old.

"So I just have to go 100 per cent. Right now, with the training I've done so far, everything has gone well. I'm trying to get away from that fear and play normally."

'I haven't changed anything technically'

There were fears Alcaraz may have had to tinker with the playing style in order to stop the problem from flaring up again - Britain's Jack Draper attempted to change his serve in a bid to get over his injury problems but remains frustratingly on the sidelines.

But Alcaraz insists he just needs competitive action.

"I haven't changed anything. I've been doing the same things. I haven't changed anything technically, in terms of my movements or the way I'm going to play," he said.

"I just wanted to feel that I was going to be myself. I knew that coming here to the US Open, being a best-of-five-set tournament and being my first tournament after such a long time, was going to be a huge challenge.

"Probably, in terms of preparation, it wasn't the ideal time. But my team and I believe that I'm ready. It wasn't an easy decision. I did everything I needed to do to be ready. I tried to do everything perfectly, both on and off the court, to feel prepared.

"We saw that everything was fine, that everything was responding properly, and we believed it was the right time to come back."

Alcaraz also admitted it is "weird" that he has not seen injured world No 1 Jannik Sinner in several months, saying: "It's a weird situation to be honest. I just wish him all the best... a great recovery and to see him back in court at his best."

'A lifetime experience' watching Spain win World Cup

Alcaraz was not entirely out of the limelight during his time away from the court, after carrying the World Cup trophy onto the pitch at the MetLife Stadium before Spain's win over Argentina.

"For me it was a lifetime experience, seeing Spain winning the World Cup," he said.

"Louis Vuitton had the trunks that was carrying the trophy, so they told me that I'm down to do it. And, I mean, it was a lifetime experience for me, like holding the trophy in the ceremony, to give it to them, you know, on the field. So it was a great experience."
