articles.title: Roger Federer tells CNN Sports he’s prepared for happy tears at Hall of Fame induction
articles.summary: The first time he cried after a big win, Roger Federer says he didn’t understand what was happening.
articles.body: The first time he cried after a big win, Roger Federer says he didn’t understand what was happening. It was 2001 at Wimbledon, and he’d just dethroned the great Pete Sampras on his Centre Court debut. “I go to my knees, (then) I shake hands with Pete and he’s my hero … and these emotions came all over me,” he told CNN Sports. “And I was like, ‘What is going on?’ This is not who I am normally.” From that moment until his tearful farewell in 2022, Federer carved out one of the most remarkable careers in tennis history and became arguably the most famous crier in sports. This weekend the Swiss superstar is being inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame, and it sounds like he’s expecting the waterworks to return. “If I’m speaking about the game and all the gratitude that I have, and having my entire family there – from my parents to my wife to my four children and my whole team from coaching staff and physios, etc. I think it could hit home very hard,” he said hours ahead of his big moment in Newport, Rhode Island. “If it happens, it will be more memorable for me personally, but I hope I get through the speech without too many hiccups. We’ll see.” For his army of fans, Federer’s induction has been a long time coming. It’s been an obvious destination since 2004, when he captured three of the four grand slam singles titles and ascended to the top of the world rankings, remaining at the summit for an extraordinary 237 consecutive weeks – still a record. In 2005, he won over 95% of his matches, but 2006 is considered to have been his peak season: Another trio of major championships and a total of 12 titles won with a record of 92-5 – a 94.8%-win rate. Few thought Sampras’ record of 14 grand slam titles would ever be broken, but Federer blew past him at Wimbledon in 2009 and never looked back. He was beloved for his grace and elegance on the court and his easy-going manner off it. Federer doesn’t have any regrets, except perhaps for the perception that he sometimes made it look too easy. “It looked like I wasn’t actually hitting the ball so hard,” he recalled how others viewed his style as a youth player. “But it was kind of flying off of my racket with a lot of power. People always thought, like, ‘It’s so simple for you,’ because it looked like elastic. But it wasn’t the case. There was a lot of work and effort put into it. “When I would lose, they say, ‘Why don’t you try harder?’ And when you win, they would say, ‘Oh my God, it’s so easy for you!’” Perhaps within that answer lies the clue to all those famed tears. “The sacrifice was massive and I was holding a lot of pressure in.” It doesn’t sound like he misses it all that much. He is at peace with his career. There is no void that needs to be filled, no desire to recreate all that pressure or those emotions. “I’m actually really happy going through everyday life at a lower pace,” he said. Life as a father of four, a philanthropist, an investor and businessman is certainly enough to keep him on his toes, and in any case, he still gets to travel: “I’ve always been a guy who loves being on the road.” His Hall of Fame induction is a chance to relive some of his greatest memories. He has enjoyed the thought of being able to play some of the other legends that he now sits alongside – should the Tennis gods permit it. “I would have a little list,” he declared, before rattling off the names of Rod Laver, Bjorn Borg, John McEnroe, Stefan Edberg, Boris Becker, and Sampras, again. “I think these would be my favorite players to play against. I’ve always admired their personalities, what they have achieved, and what they represent in the game.” Federer’s once-record haul of 20 grand slam titles has been surpassed by both Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic, but his fans will always regard him as the greatest player of all time. Having mastered the game of tennis, CNN wondered what else he would consider himself to be good at. “I’m trying to get better at golf,” he mused, “I would love to start with an instrument again. I used to play the piano, so when I have more time, I’d like to dive into that because my four children and my wife play the piano. “I hope I’m a good listener and a good decision-maker. Hopefully I’m a guy who people enjoy being around. I’m a big family guy. I love being surrounded by my friends – that’s really the priority in my life.”

articles.title: Arthur Fery: Britain's Wimbledon hero reaches Winston-Salem Open final after his opponent James Duckworth retires injured
articles.summary: Britain's Arthur Fery reaches maiden career ATP final at Winston-Salem Open where he will take on Peruvian Ignacio Buse live on Sky Sports Tennis, Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app from 9pm Saturday; watch the US Open which starts on Sunday at 3pm
articles.body:
Fery has paved his way through the ATP 250 event with a couple of routine wins over Cruz Hewitt and qualifier Mees Rottgering, and then a three-set victory over Aleksandar Kovacevic in the quarterfinals

And the 24-year-old advanced to the final after Australian James Duckworth - a player he also defeated in Cincinnati just two weeks ago - retired through injury with Fery leading 6-4 1-2.

"I'm really happy to be in the final," said Fery. "Obviously, not the way I wanted it to end at all. I hope James is going to rest up and get ready for next week but very happy to be through.

"I played well in the first set. He was serving very well and tricky but managed to get the break and from then on I thought I was playing good.

"He was hindered at the start of the second set and I saw it. It's never easy playing someone who you know is physically challenged, but overall it felt good apart from that last forehand."

The Briton went on a fairy-tale Wimbledon semi-final run earlier this summer and he is set for a new career high Monday. Eight weeks ago, Fery was ranked outside the top 100.

articles.title: Winston-Salem Open: Arthur Fery into first ATP Tour final as James Duckworth retires
articles.summary: Arthur Fery is into his first ATP Tour final as opponent James Duckworth retires because of injury at the Winston-Salem Open.
articles.body:
Britain's Arthur Fery has reached his first ATP Tour final after opponent James Duckworth retired because of injury at the Winston-Salem Open.

The 24-year-old was leading 6-4 2-1 in the semi-final when his Australian opponent, who called for a medical timeout after the first set, forfeited the match.

Fery is the first Briton to reach the final of the ATP 250 event and his progress continues after his surprise run to the Wimbledon semi-finals in July.

He has also reached a career high of 33 in the world and overtaken Cameron Norrie to become British number one.

"I am really happy to be in the final," said Fery.

"Not the way I wanted it to end at all. I hope James will get well soon and rest up for next week. But I am very happy to be through."

Fery faces Ignacio Buse in Saturday's final in North Carolina after the 22-year-old beat France's Benjamin Bonzi 6-2 4-6 6-1.

Peru's Buse, who is ranked 36th in the world, will be aiming to win his second title of the season after beating Tommy Paul at the ATP 500 event in Hamburg in May.

Only eight weeks ago, before Fery's remarkable run to the Wimbledon semi-finals, he was ranked outside the top 100.

His maiden ATP final appearance against Buse comes before next month's US Open, where he just missed out on being seeded.

Fery has been drawn against Italian 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti in the opening round at Flushing Meadows in New York.

articles.summary: El aficionado que subió las imágenes está recibiendo fuertes críticas por no respetar la intimidad del exnúmero 1 del tenis
articles.body: ¿Dónde están los límites del derecho a la privacidad? Una familia neerlandesa decidió acudir esta semana a la casa de Rafa Nadal en Manacor y llamar. La sorpresa para ellos fue que el propio Rafa salió a abrirles... y accedió a hacerse una foto con ellos. Una imagen que ha subido a sus redes sociales el propio padre de la familia (Peter Stokje) y en la que se ve la cara de circunstancias de Nadal. "¡GENIAL ESTO! Después de una visita a la Rafa Nadal Academy, se me ocurrió ir a buscar la preciosa casa de Rafael Nadal. Una vez encontrada pensé, voy a llamar al timbre. Y resulta que él mismo abrió la puerta", escribió Stokje, mientras acompañaba el mensaje con dos imágenes, una de una mujer y una niña pequeña junto a Nadal y otra de él mismo junto a Rafa. Las críticas por no respetar la privacidad e intimidad de Nadal no se hicieron esperar. La publicación en X tiene más de 500 comentarios. El propio Peter Stokje publicó después otro mensaje llamando "envidiosos" a quienes le criticaban: "Hermoso, todos esos (envidiosos) comentarios. Me río a carcajadas aquí en la hermosa Mallorca". También contestó directamente a uno de esos comentarios, que decía "personalmente creo que esto ya cruza la línea de lo decoroso. Llamar al domicilio privado de alguien así no se hace, a menos que hayas sido invitado". La contestación fue la siguiente: "Para tu información, él encontró esta acción espontánea justamente muy divertida. De lo contrario, habría dejado la puerta cerrada. ¡Que tengas un buen día!".

articles.title: Keep off the grass: British tennis players complain of marijuana smell at US Open
articles.summary: Britain’s US Open hopefuls have noticed the smell of marijuana wafting over the courts at Flushing Meadows from a nearby public park
articles.body:
Britain's US Open hopefuls thought they had put the grass behind them when Wimbledon finished, but the smell of it is all around Flushing Meadows and they are not happy about it.

Marijuana is legal for adults in New York and while smoking is not allowed on site, the aroma of weed wafts over some outside courts from the nearby Corona Park.

Katie Boulter, the British No 1, said: "Yeah, I have experienced it. You go down to the practice courts and down in the park courts, you do smell it a lot. I'm not a huge fan of it. I know a lot of players have complained on some of the specific courts.

"I've played on one before and I did smell it during my match. It's something that I wouldn't like to smell in the middle of my match. I'm trying to focus and then obviously, it takes you out of the moment and you really don't want to. You don't need distractions. So I wasn't a huge fan of it."

Fran Jones, the British No 3, said: "Last year I made a joke about that, in my first round, and I said to the guy: 'Is this normal?'. Because I was on the stadium, and it's next to the park. He's like: 'Yeah" and I was: 'Well, no wonder I'm playing pretty well'. This year I'll be like: 'No, lock in, lock in!"

Harriet Dart, who came through qualifying along with Jones, added: "I mean it's New York. I feel like everywhere you walk around, it's everywhere, no? It is what it is. Same for everyone."

The USTA said in a statement: "While we can't control what takes place off the grounds of the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, we continue to be vigilant as we maintain this."

Fery sails into first ATP final against Buse

Arthur Fery has reached the first ATP Tour final of his career at the Winston-Salem Open after his semi-final opponent, James Duckworth, retired due to injury.

Fery led 6-4, 1-2 when Duckworth withdrew because of an apparent right ​leg problem. The Wimbledon semi-finalist broke his Australian opponent at 4-4 in the first set, with the second set on serve until Duckworth retired.

The Briton will face Peru's Ignacio Buse in Saturday's final in North Carolina, after he edged past France's Benjamin Bonzi 6-2, 4-6, 6-1. Buse is one place above Fery in the world rankings at No 36, and is the 32nd seed at the US Open.

Fery, who narrowly missed out on being seeded in New York, faces a tough opening test on his main-draw US Open debut against the world No 14, Lorenzo Musetti. Reuters

articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz nunca antes había mostrado la equipación de la multinacional estadounidense Nike que iba a lucir en un torneo del Grand Slam antes de que este diera el pistoletazo de salida. La pasada edición del mixto del US Open jugó al lado de Emma Raducanu con un modelo antiguo y el mismo guión ha seguido cada mes de enero en las exhibiciones previas al Open de Australia. Sin embargo, el histórico dobles del martes con Serena Williams cambió los planes. Carlitos enseñó al mundo la vestimenta que lucirá durante su regreso a la competición en el último grande del curso. No había mejor escaparate que la Arthur Ashe, en plena ciudad de los rascacielos y con Serena al lado. El conjunto sin mangas del murciano está inspirado en el habitual conjunto de los New York Knicks, la franquicia local de la NBA que ha ganado el anillo de campeón en 2026 53 años después. Si a Alcaraz se le añade la malla en el brazo derecho con la que disputará sus partidos podría pasar por un escolta del equipo de baloncesto con sede en Manhattan. De hecho, el campeón de siete grandes ya sabe lo que es jugar en el Madison Square Garden, la mítica cancha de los Knicks. Lo hizo el 4 de diciembre de 2024 para derrotar al local Ben Shelton.

articles.summary: British number one Katie Boulter complains that the smell of cannabis is putting her off her game at the US Open.
articles.body:
British number one Katie Boulter has complained that the smell of cannabis is putting her off her game at the US Open.

On Sunday, the final major of the season begins at Flushing Meadows in New York, where cannabis is legal for adults aged 21 and over.

Though smoking is not permitted on site, the smell of cannabis wafts on to court from nearby Corona Park and has bothered a number of players in previous years, including Novak Djokovic and Alexander Zverev.

Boulter, who is preparing to face American wildcard Carol Young Suh Lee in the first round, says it is possible to smell cannabis "a lot" on the practice courts.

"I'm not a huge fan of it," said Boulter, the world number 60. "I know a lot of players have complained on some of the specific courts. I've played on one before and I did smell it during my match.

"It's something that I wouldn't like to smell in the middle of my match. I'm trying to focus and then obviously, it takes you out of the moment and you really don't want to.

"You don't need distractions. So yeah, I wasn't a huge fan of it."

The smell of cannabis has been a persistent issue at the US Open.

In 2022, Australian Open doubles champion Nick Kyrgios complained that a fan was triggering his asthma by smoking courtside, prompting the umpire to ask supporters to refrain.

Greece's Maria Sakkari pointed the smell out to an umpire midway through a set in 2023, later clarifying that it wasn't an excuse for her defeat.

The United States Tennis Association, which organises the event, says it works with the local police and parks department to reduce smoking on the site boundary.

It said: "While we can't control what takes place off the grounds of the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, we continue to be vigilant as we maintain this."

Britain's Fran Jones and Harriet Dart, who both qualified on Friday , have also noticed the smell.

"Last year I made a joke about that, in my first round, and I said to the guy, 'is this normal?'" said Jones, whose tournament begins against Poland's Magda Linette on Monday.

"Because I was on the stadium, and it's next to the park. He's like, 'yeah". and I was like: 'Well, no wonder I'm playing pretty well.'

"This year I'll be like 'no, lock in, lock in!'"

articles.title: US Open: Carlos Alcaraz walks back into the spotlight
articles.summary: Tennis News: NEW YORK CITY: Four months is a long time in tennis.Since Carlos Alcaraz injured his right wrist in a fateful moment in mid-April, the men’s tour, lik.
articles.body: NEW YORK CITY: Four months is a long time in tennis.Since Carlos Alcaraz injured his right wrist in a fateful moment in mid-April, the men’s tour, like the swirling seasons, has changed. Alexander Zverev won his first Grand Slam title at 29 during a fortnight when temperatures soared at Roland Garros, while world No. 1 Jannik Sinner defended his Wimbledon title. Spanish teenager Rafael Jodar shot up the ATP rankings, climbing from outside the top 500 to the brink of the world’s top 10 in less than a year.It is into this unpredictable landscape that a new-look Alcaraz walks.The 23-year-old, however, will take comfort from the fact that he returns to competitive tennis at the US Open, the Grand Slam where it all began for him. It was at this sprawling venue in New York’s Queens borough in 2022 that he claimed his maiden major crown and climbed to No. 1 in the rankings for the first time. It was here that he returned to the pinnacle again last year, defeating Sinner to claim his second US Open title.On Monday, Alcaraz, whose long, flowy locks, held back by a thin black headband, have already attracted plenty of wows from the fandom, opens against Roman Safiullin, the 29-year-old who lit up Wimbledon with his fight last month. The Russian also defeated Alcaraz in straight sets at the Paris Masters three years ago. The two most recent Masters 1000 champions, Ben Shelton and Arthur Fils, are potential quarter final opponents for second-seeded Alcaraz, who has 24-time major winner Novak Djokovic in his half.“I'm feeling great,” Alcaraz told international media at his pre-championship conference. “I think that right now it's (injury) is all in my head. I gotta trust my team, I gotta trust my people that tell me it's gonna be fine. So I just have to go 100%, and stay away from that fear.”“My team and I believe that I'm ready,” he added. “It wasn't an easy decision. I did whatever it took to be ready. I tried to do everything perfect on and off the court, really long practices, intense practices, just to see how my wrist is going to react.”Alcaraz practiced with the 23-year-old Holger Rune, the big-hitting former No. 4, in Murcia before arriving in New York.Even though Alcaraz enters the US Open after a four-month injury break and without a prior hard-court singles match, the second seed is hardly short of expectations.If anything, the last few months have underlined just how much Alcaraz, Sinner and the 39-year-old Djokovic matter to the men’s game. They are the sport’s biggest stars, the ones who put bums on seats. At Roland Garros in May-June, with Alcaraz out of tournament play and Sinner’s challenge wilting in the heat, Zverev’s title run became an uncomfortable one for the sport. The German’s two separate sets of domestic abuse allegations reshaped the way he has been covered in parts of the media.Now, with Sinner out with a dodgy right knee, the onus to carry the load for his generation falls on Alcaraz.Daniil Medvedev, the 30-year-old world No. 8, argued that if Alcaraz is at Flushing Meadows, it means he and his team are confident that the wrist has sufficiently recovered.“I don't think the wrist is going to be a problem,” he said. “It's more for the whole body itself. If he has a tough match, it could be interesting to see how he copes. It's really nice for me to see him here to play. If I have a chance, I’m going to watch his match, he's playing my friend Roman.”The sweet friendship angle aside, the tennis world’s eyes are on Alcaraz as he makes his comeback. Four months on, it is time to see if his wrist and tennis are ready.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Career turning point: “I’m literally living my dream right now”: How Coco Gauff’s victory over Venus Williams at Wimbledon changed the course of her career forever
articles.summary: International Sports News: Coco Gauff had already built a reputation as one of tennis’ brightest young prospects before Wimbledon 2019. She was a former junior world No. 1, reac.
articles.body: Coco Gauff had already built a reputation as one of tennis’ brightest young prospects before Wimbledon 2019. She was a former junior world No. 1, reached the US Open girls’ singles final at 13 and won the French Open girls’ singles title a year later. She had also made her WTA main-draw debut earlier that season. There was plenty of excitement around the 15-year-old, but she was still trying to prove that her junior success could translate to the senior level. Wimbledon gave her that opportunity in a way nobody could have predicted.Gauff entered Wimbledon qualifying ranked No. 313 and became the youngest player to qualify for the tournament’s main draw in the Open Era. Her reward was a first-round meeting with Venus Williams, a five-time Wimbledon champion and one of the players who had inspired her to play tennis. Gauff did not simply compete with her idol. She beat Williams 6-4, 6-4 and continued all the way to the fourth round. The victory immediately changed her status in tennis, turning a promising teenager into a global name and setting the foundation for everything that followed.Why was beating Venus Williams the turning point in Coco Gauff’s career?Gauff had already accomplished more than most players her age before arriving at the All England Club. Her junior achievements had made her a highly regarded prospect, while her first WTA win against Caty McNally at the Miami Open showed she could compete against professionals. Still, those results were mostly about potential. She had not yet produced a senior victory that could completely change the conversation around her.That changed when Gauff came through three rounds of Wimbledon qualifying without dropping a set. She then learned that Venus Williams would be waiting for her in the main draw. The matchup was almost impossible to script. Williams was 39 years old, a seven-time Grand Slam singles champion and a five-time Wimbledon winner. Gauff was 15 and playing in her first Grand Slam main draw.The teenager responded with remarkable composure. She won the first set 6-4 and kept her nerve when Williams tried to fight back in the second. Gauff eventually closed out another 6-4 set, and when Williams sent the final forehand into the net, the teenager dropped to the court in disbelief before breaking down in tears.“I never thought this would happen. I don’t know how to explain it. I’m literally living my dream. Not many people get to say that,” Gauff said afterward.The moment carried extra meaning because Venus was not simply another opponent. Gauff had grown up watching Venus and Serena Williams and had spoken about how much they had influenced her. After the match, she thanked Venus for everything she had done and told her that she would not be where she was without her inspiration.Williams also recognized what Gauff had just accomplished. Asked about the teenager’s future, she said, “I think the sky’s the limit, it really is,” while praising Gauff’s serving, movement and composure.The official Roland-Garros account later described the match as the one that created “a brand new superstar.” USTA also highlighted the Venus victory as the breakout win that began Gauff’s meteoric rise in 2019. Those descriptions explain why this particular match stands above her earlier junior achievements. Gauff had already shown that she could become a star. Beating Venus at Wimbledon showed that she was ready to start becoming one.How did the Wimbledon breakthrough change Coco Gauff’s path?The Venus victory would have been memorable on its own, but what Gauff did afterward made the breakthrough even more significant. She returned for the second round and defeated former Wimbledon semifinalist Magdalena Rybarikova 6-3, 6-3. Then she faced Polona Hercog and found herself in serious trouble after falling behind 6-3, 5-2. Gauff still fought back, saved two match points and eventually won 3-6, 7-6, 7-5.Her run finally ended against Simona Halep in the fourth round, but by then the teenager had already changed her career. She entered Wimbledon ranked No. 313 and climbed to No. 141 afterward. More importantly, she had gained the experience of playing deep into a Grand Slam while dealing with a level of attention that she had never experienced before.The spotlight followed her to the US Open. Gauff reached the third round after defeating Anastasia Potapova and Tímea Babos before losing to defending champion Naomi Osaka. The result showed that Wimbledon had not been a one-week fluke. She was now regularly competing with established professionals and attracting huge attention wherever she played.Her breakthrough year continued in Linz, Austria. Gauff had lost in the final round of qualifying but entered the main draw as a lucky loser after a player withdrew. She made the most of the opportunity, beating top seed Kiki Bertens and former French Open champion Jelena Ostapenko on her way to the title. At 15, she became the youngest WTA singles champion in 15 years.The ranking rise was just as remarkable. Gauff began 2019 ranked No. 685 and finished the season at No. 68. In less than a year, she had gone from a promising junior outside the world's top 600 to one of the youngest players inside the WTA's top 100.That progression is important when considering the Venus match as her turning point. Wimbledon did not suddenly create Gauff's talent. The talent was already there. What the tournament did was give her the stage to prove it against a legend, and the results that followed showed that she could handle the attention and expectations that came with that victory.How did that teenage breakthrough eventually lead to the champion Coco Gauff is today?Gauff's career continued to develop after her extraordinary 2019 season, and the teenager who once dreamed of becoming a Grand Slam champion eventually reached that milestone. She won her first major singles title at the 2023 US Open, followed by the WTA Finals in 2024 and her second Grand Slam singles title at Roland-Garros in 2025. She also reached a career-high ranking of No. 2, establishing herself among the leading players of her generation.Her latest success in 2026 has added another interesting chapter to the story. Gauff won the Cincinnati Open for the second time in August, defeating Jessica Pegula 6-2, 6-4 in the final. The victory gave her 12 career WTA singles titles and made her only the third woman, after Serena Williams and Victoria Azarenka, to win the Cincinnati WTA 1000 twice.The difference between that victory and her Wimbledon breakthrough is striking. In 2019, Gauff was a 15-year-old qualifier who had nothing to lose against one of her idols. In 2026, she is an established Grand Slam champion who enters major tournaments with opponents preparing specifically for her. The expectations have completely changed, but the competitive mindset that helped her survive that first Wimbledon run remains a major part of her game.That is ultimately why the victory over Venus deserves to be viewed as the defining turning point of Gauff's early career. It did not guarantee the trophies that came later, because those required years of development, difficult losses and constant improvement. What it gave her was something equally important at that stage: proof that she could handle the biggest occasion against one of the biggest names in tennis.Gauff arrived at Wimbledon as a 15-year-old qualifier ranked No. 313. She left as one of the sport's most talked-about young stars. Seven years later, she has two Grand Slam singles titles, a WTA Finals championship and 12 WTA singles titles, with her latest Cincinnati triumph coming in 2026.The dream she spoke about after beating Venus was only beginning to take shape. Today, Gauff is no longer the teenager hoping to prove she belongs. She is one of the players standing at the center of the sport, and it all started with the day she stunned her idol at Wimbledon.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Arthur Fery beaten in Winston-Salem Open final by Ignacio Buse
articles.summary: Arthur Fery misses out on his first ATP Tour title with a straight-set defeat by Ignacio Buse in the final of the Winston-Salem Open.
articles.body:
Arthur Fery missed out on his first ATP Tour title with a straight-set defeat by Ignacio Buse in the final of the Winston-Salem Open.

Fery, who was the talk of Wimbledon as he reached the semi-finals of his home major in July, lost 6-3 6-2 to Peru's Buse.

The 24-year-old was the first Briton to reach the final of the ATP 250 tournament in North Carolina and will rise to 33 in the world rankings as a result - overtaking Cameron Norrie as British number one.

Only eight weeks ago, before his astonishing run to the last four at the All England Club, he was ranked outside the top 100.

Little could separate Fery and Buse in the early stages of their match on Saturday, before the Peruvian took control with a break to love for a 5-3 lead.

Fery quickly fell further behind in the second set as Buse opened up a double break cushion with no reply, and while he pulled back one of those breaks, it proved to no avail as his opponent reeled off three straight games to seal the win.

For 22-year-old Buse, victory makes him the youngest ever winner of Winston-Salem and marks a second career title after he beat American Tommy Paul at the ATP 500 event in Hamburg in May.

With little time to reflect on his Winston-Salem run, Fery will now head to New York for the US Open, which starts on Sunday.

Set to play at Flushing Meadows for the first time, he faces a tough opening tie against Italian 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti.

Fery is one of nine British players set to feature in the main draws at the US Open, the final Grand Slam of the season.

Joining him in the men's draw are Norrie and Jan Choinski, qualifiers Toby Samuel and Harry Wendelken, and lucky loser Jacob Fearnley.

Katie Boulter is joined by qualifiers Fran Jones and Harriet Dart in the women's draw, but both Jack Draper and Emma Raducanu are missing through injury.

articles.title: Arthur Fery: Brits hopes of landing maiden ATP Tour title at Winston-Salem Open ended by Peruvian Ignacio Buse with US Open starting Sunday
articles.summary: Britain's Arthur Fery beaten in straight-sets by Peruvian Ignacio Buse in Winston-Salem Open final; watch the US Open from Sunday live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
From 3-3 in the first set, Fery lost six straight games before eventually going down 6-3 6-2 to Buse.

The promising 22-year-old clinched his second trophy of the season having lifted his maiden tour-level trophy at the ATP 500 event in Hamburg.

Fery was aiming to add to his already memorable season having reached the semi-finals at Wimbledon and he is set for a new career high Monday.

With his spot in the Winston-Salem final, 24-year-old Fery has moved up to a new career high of No 33 in the live rankings, overtaking Cameron Norrie as the British No 1 in doing so.

Eight weeks ago, Fery was outside the top 100.

"Congratulations to you and your team, Ignacio, for your second title this year," Fery said during the trophy ceremony. "I want to thank my team as well. It couldn't be us today but thank you for everything you do for me. We have had a great year and hopefully we can finish strong."

Speaking to Sky Sports , former British No 1 Tim Henman said he has been impressed with Fery's showing in North Carolina.

Fery, who is set to make his main draw debut at the US Open starting on Sunday, faces a tough task against Italy's world No 14 Lorenzo Musetti in the opening round .

"He's had a great week, but that's his level," said Henman. "On the back of making the semi-finals at Wimbledon, he's a top 30 player, so getting through to the final of tour events and hopefully winning them is what he's about now.

"Yes, he has a tough match against Musetti. He goes into that match as a clear underdog but he's confident."

Buse delivered a composed performance to secure his triumph in just 77 minutes, with Fery unable to match the relentless pace.

"It is very special for me," Buse said in his post-match interview. "With all my team, we have been working very, very hard. Some things are very tough that we go through as tennis players, but I also want to congratulate Arthur and his team."

articles.title: El emocionante discurso de Federer en el Salón de la Fama
articles.standfirst: Su mujer Mirka, Navratilova, Hingis y sus rivales, protagonistas de las emotivas palabras del suizo
articles.summary: Su mujer Mirka, Navratilova, Hingis y sus rivales, protagonistas de las emotivas palabras del suizo
articles.body: Muy emocionado y al borde de las lágrimas en varias ocasiones, el suizo Roger Federer dio este sábado las gracias a su mujer, Mirka, por acompañarle en su vida, a Martina Navratilova por ser fuente de inspiración, y recordó el legado de Rafa Nadal y Novak Djokovic en su discurso de casi media hora en el día en el que entró al Salón de la Fama del tenis. "Cuando cierro mis ojos y pienso en el juego que amo. Esto es lo que veo. Estoy en Basilea y tengo 13 años. No estoy jugando, soy un recogepelotas. Veo el juego y nunca olvidaré cómo veía a los jugadores luchar ante adversidades, la intensidad. Quiero dar las gracias a todos los recogepelotas que han estado en mis partidos durante horas. Los veo, les doy las gracias, y yo fui como ustedes", empezó Federer. El suizo recordó que tenía tres años cuando tocó su primera raqueta. Era de su padre y era de madera. A partir de ahí contó sus días jugando al tenis, los momentos pasados con su familia acudiendo a torneos y trabajando para convertirse en jugador profesional. Se conmovió al nombrar a sus entrenadores, en particular Severin Lüthi, con el que estuvo 18 años. "Severin Lüthi es el técnico que he tenido más tiempo, 18 largos años juntos, me mantuvo motivado cuando lo necesitaba y me protegió cuando necesitaba que se me protegiera", dijo, antes de emocionarse. Entre sus fuentes de inspiración nombró a su compatriota Martina Hingis y a Martina Navratilova. "Hingis, suiza como yo, número uno del mundo desde los 16 años, algo que yo no hice. Navratilova en mi casa es famosa por haberme inspirado a jugar al tenis. Martina inspiró a Mirka, y Mirka me inspiró a mí. Ella es mi mujer, pero eso se queda corto: es mi entrenadora, mi estilista, la persona que me enseñó a estar más concentrado en el tenis y disfrutar de todo lo demás. Es una gran madre. Ella y yo nos damos la mano y atravesamos muros. Ella es todo esto", afirmó. "El tenis es algo complejo y bonito, es un espectáculo de ver. Hay mucha presión en el tenis, un volcán de presión, de emociones, y cuando el partido terminaba probablemente ustedes veían lo que sentía dentro. El tenis significó todo para mí: crear algo nuevo, es mi mentalidad", añadió. "Fuera de la cancha, la amistad en el vestuario, jugar a las cartas hasta el segundo previo al partido... Algunos rivales se volvieron amigos y nos conectamos de por vida. Esos son de los mejores recuerdos que encontré en el ATP Tour. También había otro juego, el que se vive con amigos y familia. Con Mirka empezamos a hacer cosas como jugar videojuegos y cenar con amigos. Luego empezamos a cambiar pañales. Nuestros hijos nos inspiran y nos hacen felices cada día", recordó. "Mi tiempo en el tenis terminó, pero el tenis siempre estará en la intersección de todo lo que me interesa", concluyó. "El Salón de la Fama muestra la evolución del tenis y estoy orgulloso de ser parte de él. Estoy contento de haber pasado por generaciones, desde (Pete) Sampras hasta las rivalidades épicas con Andy (Murray), Novak (Djokovic) y Rafa (Nadal)", dijo. "Nosotros dejaremos la pista, pero el deporte sigue. Espero que el deporte mantenga un poco de ese espíritu y afición. Espero que los jugadores sigan con esa camaradería entre ellos, que sean fieles a su verdadera identidad, que no dejen de tomar riesgos, que sigan empujando este deporte y que sigan mejorando, mejorando y mejorando", añadió.

articles.title: US Open predictions: Carlos Alcaraz and Coco Gauff? The Sky Sports Tennis panel pick their winners and dark horses ahead of the Grand Slam in New York
articles.summary: Who are the winners and dark horses for this year's US Open at Flushing Meadows? watch the final Grand Slam of 2026 from Sunday at 3pm live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
Tim Henman, Laura Robson, Ryan Harrison, Naomi Broady and Martina Navratilova are just some of the names who have picked their winners for this year's final Grand Slam of the year.

Sascha Zverev: He's gone up a level since winning his first Grand Slam title at the French Open and I reflect on his improvements in the last 12 months. He's so much more aggressive, proactive, taking the ball on from the back of the court. His serve is so consistent and I think this is so much more wide open because Jannik Sinner is not here and Carlos Alcaraz is coming back from a long injury lay-off so I think he has confidence to take advantage.

Aryna Sabalenka: She hasn't been playing particularly well but I think a player of her stature when she gets to the Grand Slams and the biggest and best events you find that there's an extra gear to her game and there's also an extra intensity to her focus and concentration. You go back to that old saying: Form is temporary, class is permanent.

Arthur Fils: I did choose Fils when he was in the quarter-finals of Cincinnati so for him to go on and take the title there, I mean that's a huge step up and he's struggled with injury so potentially seven best-of-five-set matches, he's got to stay healthy but he's got a good shot.

Alex Eala: Unbelievable competitor. The improvement she's made in her game and add to that the support that she has, she really is great to watch. I love her attitude and that spirit. So as an outsider I'm very happy with that pick.

Novak Djokovic: I think it's a great opportunity. He's had a couple of losses and didn't look amazing in Cincinnati but if you look at the way he's played at the majors. I'm throwing out the one on clay because clay has never been his favourite surface but if you look at his last hardcourt major he made the Australian Open final and was a set up on Carlos Alcaraz. I think Novak goes all the way!

Coco Gauff: I expect her to continue on her trend of hot form.

Lerner Tien: He's been in great form and won a lot of matches and he's got the right emotional temperament in three-out- of-five-sets. He's also had some big wins at the Australian Open.

Sorana Cirstea: It's been a great year for her and it's a year which she said is going to be her last on season and probably her best year ever. I just think coming in for potentially the last major of her career, it just feels like a good Cinderella story.

Arthur Fils: He's in form. He possibly would have won a Grand Slam now had he not had the injuries that he had. His trajectory is so high.

Iga Swiatek: She's Iga. She's playing really well, and I think her ball does a lot of damage on these lively hard courts with the spin and I just feel over the last few weeks she's got her star power back a bit.

Ben Shelton: American. Playing well. Home crowd. He will really vibe off the energy.

Marta Kostyuk: She's had a great year. I feel like the next thing to put in her hat would be a Slam.

Carlos Alcaraz: Surely he's the favourite coming into the tournament!? As long as he's fit and healthy then I think he's going to be absolutely fine. Almost always with the multiple Slam champions, whether it's been Serena Williams or Rafael Nadal, or whoever it is... whenever they turn up, you go 'Oh yeah, they're just exactly how they've always been'. Maybe it takes a match or two to get there, but I'm confident he's going to be great.

Jessica Pegula: She's playing great and she's going to put herself in a great position as she always does. Super consistent and if other players just have a wobble at the wrong moment they get themselves taken out or don't perform against Pegula then she's going to be ready to pounce. She's been a finalist before and she's super consistent.

Ann Lee: She's had a sneaky good season. She's been moving up the rankings and she's seeded coming into the US Open. She's an American player with lovely shots and she's been settling into life on tour. I project bigger and better things for her. I think she's a great talent. She could be playing Aryna Sabalenka in the quarter-finals.

Thiago Tirante: He is one of my absolute favourite players. He hits the ball harder than anyone out there. He hit a 120mph forehand earlier this year with his serve at around 145mph. He's such an exciting player. There's no way he cannot be in the top 20. He's going to be great!

Arthur Fils: Cincinnati has been a pretty good marker for form but it's a wild prediction, asking him to go seven best-of-five matches so relatively fresh from his injury, having missed so many Grand Slams. Could he win this US Open? In the absence of Sinner and the uncertainly of Alcaraz he's absolutely in the conversation.

Coco Gauff: She won in Cincinnati and then won the US Open in 2023 so why can't she do it again this year. I've been of the opinion that it will all come together for her in the sense that these technical deficiencies that we so often discuss and see on the court in front of our eyes will not so much disappear but will become less obvious.

I find it hard to believe Gauff will go her entire career with continued deficiencies.

Frances Tiafoe: I like the way he has knuckled down and increased the professionalism. The off-court work he has done has been rewarded. He knows he can go the distance and with some form coming in, I think he could be one to watch.

Iva Jovic: She's a terrific young player and is a Grand Slam winner in the future. This one might be too soon for her but you just never know how the draw might open up.

articles.title: US Open key questions: Gigi Salmon dissects the draws with Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic, Aryna Sabalenka and Coco Gauff in the mix
articles.summary: Gigi Salmon dissects the men's and women's draws ahead of the US Open; who will the presenter pick as her winners for the titles in New York?; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
It's also played on a surface where more players fancy their chances; many have love-hate relationships with clay and grass but hard courts are their bread and butter.

The US Open is now a three-week event, week one is fan week, which this year saw five-time champion Roger Federer return for an exhibition, Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik win their first Grand Slam title after being crowned mixed doubles champions - in a competition that saw a return to Flushing Meadows of six-time champion Serena Williams - and the qualifying competition, which started with 15 Brits in the draw.

The main draw starts on Sunday and contains nine Brits, with a record five coming through qualifying. The men's competition is headed up by Sascha Zverev in the absence of Jannik Sinner [knee injury] and the women's by world No 1 Aryna Sabalenka.

In terms of questions to be asked, there are five main ones...

How will the wrist of returning champion Carlos Alcaraz hold up under the pressure of best-of-five-set Grand Slam play?

Will 39-year-old Novak Djokovic finally get his hands on Grand Slam title No 25?

Can an American finally win the men's title in New York? The last to do it was Andy Roddick in 2003.

Can Aryna Sabalenka make history and win the US Open title for a third consecutive year? It's something that hasn't been done since Serena Williams in 2012-14.

And maybe more importantly... who will end the tournament as world No 1, with four players in the running?

If we break down the draws starting with the men, the top half is headed up in the absence of Sinner by Zverev, top seed at a Grand Slam for the first time and with a major title under his belt having won the French Open earlier this year.

The draw has been kind to the German, who will fancy his chances and comes into the tournament with an 18-2 record at Grand Slam level this year.

The question, as always, is how will he cope with the pressure having fallen early in both Masters 1000 events in the lead-up as the top seed.

Working from top to bottom, the second quarter is headed up by the Australian and sixth seed Alex de Minaur, projected to meet Zverev in the quarter-finals. He might not have Djokovic or Alcaraz in his section but he does have former finalist Taylor Fritz, French Open finalist Flavio Cobolli and last year's semi-finalist Felix Auger-Aliassime.

The bottom half is absolutely stacked and features all five former US Open champions in Alcaraz, Djokovic, Daniil Medvedev, Stan Wawrinka and Marin Cilic.

Working our way down next up is Djokovic's quarter, which features Medvedev, finalist in Cincinnati Francis Tiafoe, finalist in Canada Brandon Nakashima, and a second-round meeting with one of Wawrinka or Matteo Berrettini. That's before any talk of a meeting with Alcaraz - the defending champion who heads up the final quarter.

The seeds in the Alcaraz section include winner in Canada, Ben Shelton, winner in Cincinnati, Arthur Fils, Alexander Bublik, Tommy Paul and big-hitting Roman Safiullin, who has beaten him before and is, for me, one of his toughest tests for the Spaniard having not played a singles match since April.

Into the women's draw with each quarter containing very different stories...

The main story involving Sabalenka in the first quarter who is not only looking to try and become the first woman since Serena Williams to win three consecutive US Open titles but she's also trying to hold on to the world No 1 ranking.

On paper her draw isn't too bad until the quarter-finals, where she could face Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova.

The worry is Sabalenka's lack of form going 17-7 since April and not having won a title since March. She is without a Grand Slam title so far in 2026 and is looking vulnerable.

The second quarter is headlined by Jessica Pegula who is in contention to end the tournament as world No 1. For that to happen, the former finalist would need to win the title; nothing less would do.

Dangers lie around every corner for Pegula with Elina Svitolina, Karolina Muchova and Sorana Cirstea in her section and a second-round meeting with one of former Australian Open Champion Sofia Kenin or two-time US Open Champion Venus Williams.

Former US Open champion and current Cincinnati champion Coco Gauff heads up the top of the bottom half; she also has a chance of reaching world No 1, but only if she wins the title.

Lying in wait for her in the third quarter are last year's finalist Amanda Anisimova, French Open Champion Mirra Andreeva, Washington champion Alex Eala, and a potentially tricky early meeting with Paula Badosa.

And finally, to what surely is the toughest quarter of the draw with Elena Rybakina, Iga Swaitek, Naomi Osaka, Madison Keys and Belinda Bencic.

Rybakina will be the new world No 1 if she reaches the semi-finals, that is in her hands. What isn't is the left ankle/Achilles injury that she has been managing for a while, but flared up in Cincinnati forcing her to withdraw in her match against Swiatek. She has looked tentative in practice, so only time will tell if it will hold up to allow her to reach world No 1 for the first time in her career.

When it comes to the Brits, a word on Arthur Fery, who in his second tournament since reaching the semi-finals of Wimbledon this summer, reached the final of Winston-Salem - losing out to third seed Ignacio Buse in the title decider .

Perfect preparation for Fery who has had a whirlwind summer and now heads to New York as the British No 1 thanks to that run.

The Brit will be making his debut at the US Open and it's a tough one up against 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti.

Musetti recently found some form in Cincinnati but isn't long back from a back injury, so Fery will fancy his chances.

Fery sits in the top quarter draw with top seed Zverev. Also in that section is Jan Choinski, who takes on the Dutchman Botic Van De Zandschulp.

And the other Brit to qualify on ranking is Cameron Norrie, who is in the bottom half with Alcaraz. He is the 29th seed and faces the Frenchman Luca van Assche, for the right to take on Miomir Kecmanovic or Dennis Shapovalov in round two.

In total, there are nine Brits in the main draw and for the first time at the US Open five having come through qualifying.

Among them is Toby Samuel, the world No 110, who will make his US Open main draw debut, with the 23-year-old having drawn the Czech Tomas Machac, the world No 58.

Harry Wendleken is also set for his debut after playing nine sets and nine hours to reach the main draw, and his reward is the 21st seed Luciano Darderi. Jacob Fearnley, in as a lucky loser for his second US Open appearance, will take on the Spaniard Martin Landaluce.

In the women's draw, Katie Boulter was the only direct entrant and has been handed a good first round up against the American wild card Carol Young Suh Lee.

Lee is 24, sitting at her career-high ranking of 140, and will be making her Grand Slam main draw debut.

Should Boulter win, then more than likely she will face US Open mixed doubles champion and Wimbledon finalist Karolina Muchova in round two.

Joining Boulter through the qualifying route is Harriet Dart, who beat Heather Watson in the final round to set up a meeting with the American and world No 54 Peyton Stearns, who she recently played and lost to in Cincinnati, but did beat the American in US Open qualifying in 2021.

And Fran Jones, who for a second year running has secured qualification into the main draw where she will face Magda Linette of Poland in what will be a first meeting between the two.

Also a reminder that we haven't seen the last of Serena Williams at the US Open this year.

After playing with Alcaraz in the mixed doubles she is teaming up with sister Venus in the doubles after getting a wild card.

The two-time US Open doubles champions last played a Grand Slam together in 2022 at Flushing Meadows.

And just a word on the prize money, which has risen again this year: the men's and women's singles champions will get $5.5m (£4.7m) each and for reaching the first round it's a guaranteed $140,000 (£120,000).

I have left it as late as possible, and I'm still not convinced, but for who's going to win.

I will say Zverev to win his second Grand Slam title. It was tough to go against him once I saw what looks like a very favourable draw and for the women I am going outside of those who could end the tournament as world No 1 and pick Naomi Osaka to win her third US Open and first here since 2020.

From Sunday, the Sky Sports Tennis team will be back together for 15 days of wall-to-wall action with every ball of every match on every court available for you to enjoy.

Hear from Martin Navratilova, Tim Henman, Marion Bartoli, Laura Robson, Ryan Harrison and Naomi Broady to name just a few.

We look forward to your company this Sunday from 3pm live from New York.
